<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
    There exists a mapping class group invariant complex hyperK\"ahler structure $(g,\mathbf i, \mathbb I, \mathbb J, \mathbb K)$ on $\mathbb{M}_0(S)$, where $\mathbf i$ is the almost-complex structure of $\mathbb{M}_0(S)$, such that:
    \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em]
    \item The tensors $(-(i/2)g,\mathbf i, \mathbb I, \mathbf i\mathbb I)$ restrict to the Loustau-Sanders complex bi-K\"ahler structure on the complex embedding of $\mathcal{QF}(S)$.
        \item  The tensors $(g,\mathbb I, \mathbb J, \mathbb K)$ restrict to Donaldson's hyperK\"ahler structure on the totally real embedding of $\mathcal{AF}(S)$.
        \item  The tensors $(g,\mathbb I, \mathbf i\mathbb J, \mathbf i\mathbb K)$ restrict to the para-hyperK\"ahler structure of Mazzoli-Seppi-Tamburelli on the totally real embedding of $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$. 
    \end{enumerate}
    Moreover, $\mathcal{QF}(S)$, $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ are all totally geodesic in $\mathbb{M}_0(S)$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm: local biholos intro}
    There exists a quotient space $\mathbb{M}(S)$ of $\mathrm M^*(S)$, which is a complex manifold of complex dimension $6|\chi(S)|$, such that the following two maps :
    \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
        \item the map $\mathrm M^*(S)\to T^*\mathcal T(S)\times T^*\mathcal T(\overline{S})$ associating to the 5-tuple
        $(J_1,q_1, -J_2, \overline{q_2}, u)$
        the pairs $[J_1,q_1]\in T^*\mathcal T(S)$ and $[-J_2,\overline{q_2}]\in T^*\mathcal T(\overline{S})$, and
        \item the holonomy map $\mathrm M^*(S)\to\chi\big(\pi_1(S), \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})\times \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})\big)$
    \end{itemize} 
    descend to  well-defined and locally biholomorphic maps on $\mathbb{M}(S)$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:area intro}
    The complex area functional $\mathcal A:\mathbb M_0(S)\to\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$ is a Hamiltonian function with respect to $\omega_{\mathbb I}$, that is:
    $$\mathrm d\mathcal A=\omega_{\mathbb I}(\xi,\cdot)$$
    where $\xi$ is the infinitesimal generator of the (local) $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}^*$-action.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
\label{def:holomorphic_riemannian_metric}
A \emph{holomorphic Riemannian metric} $\operatorname{\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle}$ on $\mathbb X$ is a holomorphic section of $\mathrm{Sym}^2(T^{*1,0}\mathbb X)$ that at every point gives a non-degenerate bi-linear form on $T^{1,0}\mathbb{X}$. The pair $(\mathbb X, \operatorname{\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle})$ is called a \emph{holomorphic Riemannian manifold}.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
\label{def:homorphic levi-civita}
The \emph{holomorphic Levi-Civita connection} of a holomorphic Riemannian manifold $(\mathbb X, \operatorname{\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle})$ is the unique affine connection on $T\mathbb X$ whose natural $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$--linear extension
\[
D : \Gamma(\mathbb{C} T\mathbb{X}) \times \Gamma(\mathbb{C} T\mathbb{X}) \longrightarrow \Gamma(\mathbb{C} T\mathbb{X}), \qquad D_U V := D(U,V)~,
\]
satisfies the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $T^{1,0} \mathbb{X}$ is $D$--invariant, i.e. $D_U(\Gamma(T^{1,0} \mathbb{X})) \subset \Gamma(T^{1,0} \mathbb{X})$ for every $U \in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T\mathbb{X})$;
    \item The restriction of $D$ over $\Gamma(T^{1,0} \mathbb{X})$ is torsion-free, i.e.
    \[
    D_{V}W - D_W V = [V,W] 
    \]
    for all $V, W \in \Gamma(T^{1,0}\mathbb{X})$.
    \item For every holomorphic local section $Z$ of $T^{1,0}\mathbb{X}$ and for any $U \in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T\mathbb{X})$,
    \[
    D_{\mathbf{i}U} Z = \mathbf{i}(D_U Z)~.
    \]
    \item $D$ is compatible with the metric $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$, i.e.
    \[
    W(\langle U, V \rangle) = \langle D_W U, V \rangle + \langle U, D_W V \rangle
    \]
    for any $U, V, W \in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T \mathbb{X})$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Property (1) is equivalent to asking that the ($\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$--linear extension of the) almost-complex structure $\mathbf{i}$ is $D$--parallel. Properties (1) and (2) imply that, given any section $V \in \Gamma(T^{1,0} \mathbb{X})$, the $(0,1)$--part of $D_\bullet V$ coincides with $\bar{\partial} V$, where $\bar{\partial}$ denotes the del-bar operator of the holomorphic vector bundle $T^{1,0}\mathbb{X}$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
The natural identification between $T_J\mathcal C(S)$ and $T_{J_0}^{1,0}\mathcal C(S)\cong \mathrm{Belt}_{J_0}(S)$ corresponds to the map
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:ident mu Jdot}
    \dot J\mapsto \dot\mu=\frac{1}{4i}\left(\dot{J} - i J \dot{J}\right)~.
    \end{equation}
    As a consequence, the almost-complex structure of $\mathcal{C}(S)$ acts on $T_J\mathcal{C}(S)$ by
        \begin{equation}\label{eq:J to Jdot}
    \dot J\mapsto J\dot{J}~.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Any local complex coordinate $z$ for $(S,J)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:def_complex_chart}
    \mathrm{d}z\circ J= i\,\mathrm{d}z~, \qquad \mathrm{d}\overline z \circ J=-i\,\mathrm{d}\overline z~,
\end{equation}
or, equivalently,
\[
J(\partial_{\overline z})=-i\,\partial_{\overline z}~, \qquad J(\partial_z)=i\,\partial_z~.
\]
Now, a smooth path of complex structures on $S$ corresponds to a smooth $1$-parameter family of endomorphisms $(J_{t})_t$ and, by the Generalized Riemann mapping theorem, we can find a corresponding family of local coordinates $z_t$ for $(S,J_t)$ varying regularly in $t$. Differentiating Equation~\eqref{eq:def_complex_chart} at $t=0$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{d}\dot z\circ J+ \mathrm{d}z\circ \dot{J} &= i \,\mathrm{d}\dot z~, \\
    \mathrm{d}\dot {\overline z}\circ J+ \mathrm{d}\overline z\circ \dot{J} &= -i\, \mathrm{d}\dot {\overline z}~,
\end{align*}
and, evaluating in $\partial_{\overline z}$ e $\partial_z$, we deduce
\begin{align}\label{eq: descrizione dot J}
   \mathrm{d}z(\dot{J}\partial_{\overline z})&= 2i\,\partial_{\overline z} \dot z~, & \mathrm{d}\overline z (\dot{J}\partial_{\overline z})& = 0~, \\
   \mathrm{d}z(\dot{J}\partial_z) & = 0~, & \mathrm{d}\overline z(\dot{J}\partial_z) & = -2i \,\partial_z\dot{\overline z}~. \notag
\end{align}
By construction, the tensor
\begin{equation}
\label{eq: diff di Beltrami}
    \dot{\mu} := \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial_{\overline z} z_t}{\partial_z z_t} \frac {\mathrm{d}\overline z}{\mathrm{d}z} \right)= \partial_{\overline z}\dot z \frac {\mathrm{d}\overline z}{\mathrm{d}z} = \frac 1 {2i} \mathrm{d}z(\dot{J}\partial_{\overline z})  \frac {\mathrm{d}\overline z}{\mathrm{d}z}:=\dot{\mu}_{z}\,\frac {\mathrm{d}\overline z}{\mathrm{d}z}~,
\end{equation}
is the first-order variation at $t = 0$ of the Beltrami differential of the identity maps $id : (S,J_0) \to (S,J)$ and, in particular, it is an element of $\mathrm{Belt}_{J_0}(S)$. From Equation~\eqref{eq: descrizione dot J}, we deduce that $\dot{J}$ can be written in local coordinates as
\[
\dot{J} = \mathrm{d}\overline{z}(\dot{J} \partial_z) \, \partial_{\bar{z}} \otimes \mathrm{d}z + \mathrm{d}z(\dot{J} \partial_{\bar{z}}) \, \partial_z \otimes \mathrm{d}\overline{z}~.
\]
Similarly, 
\[
- i \, J \dot{J} = - \mathrm{d}\overline{z}(\dot{J} \partial_z) \,\partial_{\bar{z}} \otimes \mathrm{d}z + \mathrm{d}z(\dot{J} \partial_{\bar{z}}) \,\partial_z \otimes \mathrm{d}\overline{z}~.
\]
Therefore, combining the two expressions above with Equation~\eqref{eq: diff di Beltrami}, we have
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{2}\left(\dot{J} - i J \dot{J}\right) & = \mathrm{d}z(\dot{J} \partial_{\bar{z}}) \, \partial_z \otimes \mathrm{d}\overline{z}=2i\,\dot{\mu}~.
\end{align*}
    This proves the formula \eqref{eq:ident mu Jdot}. The formula \eqref{eq:J to Jdot} then follows from the immediate check that multiplication of $\dot\mu$ by $i$ corresponds to pre-composition of $\dot J$ by $J$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- defn-3: body_md -->
A \emph{complex metric} $g$ on a smooth (real) surface $S$ is a smooth section of $\mathrm{Sym}^2(\mathbb C T^*S)$ which is pointwise non-degenerate. More precisely, $g$ is a non-degenerate symmetric $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$--bilinear form defined on $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T_pS$, for all $p\in S$, which varies smoothly with the point.
<!-- end defn-3 -->
<!-- defn-4: body_md -->
\label{def conformal metrics}
    Two complex metrics $g$ and $\widehat g$ on a smooth surface $S$ are \emph{conformal} if there exists a smooth function $\varrho\colon S\to \mathbb C^*$ such that $\hat g=\varrho \, g$.
<!-- end defn-4 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
\label{def: positive}
    A complex metric $g$ is \emph{positive} if for each $p\in S$, the two isotropic directions are contained in distinct components of $\mathbb P_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T_pS)\setminus \mathbb P_\mathbb R(T_pS)$.
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
\label{def: bicomplex structure} A {bi-complex structure} on $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS$ is a $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$--linear bundle endomorphism $\mathcal J:\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS\to\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\mathcal J^2=-\mathrm{Id}$;
    \item for all $p\in S$, the eigenspaces $V_i(\mathcal J_p)$ and $V_{-i}(\mathcal J_p)$ of $\mathcal J$ relative to the eigenvalues $\pm i$ lie respectively in the positive and in the negative connected component of $\mathbb P_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T_pS)\setminus \mathbb P_\mathbb R(T_pS)$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:unique_bicomplex_structure}
Given a positive complex metric $g$ on an oriented surface $S$ there exists a unique bi-complex structure $ \mathcal J$ compatible with $g$, namely $g( \mathcal J\cdot, \mathcal J\cdot)=g$.
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop: Bers metrics holo dependence}
    Let $S$ be a closed oriented surface. The map 
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal C(S)\times\mathcal C(\overline S) &\to \mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS, \operatorname{\mathbb{C}})\\
        (J_1, -J_2) &\mapsto  \vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}~,
    \end{align*}
    has the following properties:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item The tensor $\vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}$ is a positive complex metric of constant curvature $-1$.
        \item The pair of complex structures associated to $\vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}$ are precisely $J_1$ and $-J_2$.
        \item $\vb*h(J, -J)$ is the unique hyperbolic Riemannian metric whose conformal class is $J$.
    \end{itemize}
    Moreover, when considered as a map
  between complex Fréchet manifolds, it is holomorphic.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
\label{def: admissible and positive immersion}
    Let $\sigma:\Sigma\to\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ be an immersion. The pull-back bilinear form $\mathtt I:=\sigma^*{\operatorname{\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle}}$ is called the (complex) \emph{first fundamental form} of $\sigma$. Moreover, we say that:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item  $\sigma$ is \emph{admissible} if $\mathtt I$ is a complex metric on $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T\Sigma$.
        \item $\sigma$ is \emph{positive} if $\mathtt I$ is a positive complex metric on $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T\Sigma$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
Let $\sigma:\Sigma\to\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ be a positive immersion. Then:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item The \emph{complex shape operator} of $\sigma$ is the endomorphism $B$ of $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T\Sigma$ defined by $\mathrm{d}\sigma\circ B=-(DN)\circ \mathrm{d}\sigma$.
        \item The \emph{complex second fundamental form} of $\sigma$ is the symmetric bilinear form on $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T\Sigma$ defined by $\mathtt {II}=\mathtt I(B\cdot, \cdot)$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{thm: integration GC}
Let $\Sigma$ be a simply connected surface, let $\mathtt I$ be a positive complex metric with complex Levi-Civita connection $\nabla^\mathtt I$, and let $\mathtt {II}\in \mathrm{Sym}_2(\mathbb{C} T\Sigma)$. Then, there exists a positive immersion $\sigma:\Sigma\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ with $\mathtt I$ and $\mathtt {II}$ as first and second fundamental form if and only if they satisfy Equations~\eqref{eq: Gauss PSL(2,C)}-\eqref{eq: Codazzi PSL(2,C)}. 
Moreover, 
                                                                                                
$\sigma$ is unique up to post-composing with elements in $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})\times \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rmk:uniqueness post composition}
Observe that, in the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm: integration GC}, if $\sigma_1,\sigma_2\colon \Sigma\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ have the same first and second fundamental forms, then there exists exactly one isometry $\phi\in \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})\times\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ such that $\sigma_2 = \phi \circ \sigma_1$. Indeed, at any given point $p\in \Sigma$ and linearly independent $v,w\in T_p\Sigma$, the map $\phi$ is such that $(\mathrm{d}\phi)_{\sigma_1(p)}((\mathrm{d}\sigma_1)_p(v))=(\mathrm{d}\sigma_2)_p(v)$, $(\mathrm{d}\phi)_{\sigma_1(p)}((\mathrm{d}\sigma_1)_p(w))=(\mathrm{d}\sigma_2)_p(w)$ and, as a consequence of $\phi^*\Omega=\Omega$, also $(\mathrm{d}\phi)_{\sigma_1(p)}(N_{\sigma_1(p)}) = N_{\sigma_2(p)}$: these conditions completely characterize $\mathrm{d}\phi$ at $\sigma_1(p)$, hence they characterizes $\phi$ globally.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:three cases immersions}
    Let $\Sigma$ be a simply connected surface, let $\sigma\colon \Sigma\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ be a positive immersion with fundamental forms $\mathtt I$ and $\mathtt {II}$.                                                                                                                         
    Then, up to composing $\sigma$ with elements in $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2$:
    \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em]
        \item $\sigma(\Sigma)\subset \mathbb G$ if and only if $\mathtt {II}=0$.
        \item $\sigma(\Sigma)\subset\mathbb H^3$ if and only if $\mathtt I$ is a (real-valued) Riemannian metric and $\mathtt {II}$ is real-valued. In this case, $\mathtt I$ and $\mathtt {II}$ coincide with the usual fundamental forms in hyperbolic geometry. 
        \item $\sigma(\Sigma)\subset\mathbb{A}\mathrm{d}\mathbb{S}^3$ if and only if $\mathtt I$ is a (real-valued) Riemannian metric and $i\mathtt {II}$ is real-valued. In this case, $\mathtt I$ and $i\mathtt {II}$ coincide with the usual fundamental forms in Anti-de Sitter geometry. 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rmk: af e mgh 1}
Let us briefly comment on these three items in terms of the Gauss-Codazzi equations~\eqref{eq: Gauss PSL(2,C)}-\eqref{eq: Codazzi PSL(2,C)}. 

In the case of item (1), we have $\mathtt {II}=0$, so by Equation~\eqref{eq: Gauss PSL(2,C)} the first fundamental form $\mathtt I$ has constant curvature -1. We thus recover the fact, already mentioned in Section~\ref{sec: Bers metrics}, that Bers metrics have constant curvature $-1$: in fact, they are obtained by pull-back of the metric of $\widetilde{\mathbb G}$ from an immersion of $\Sigma$ into $\widetilde{\mathbb G}$, so, after composing with the projection $\widetilde{\mathbb G}\to\mathbb G$ (which is a local isometry), the first fundamental form is realized as in item (1). 

For item (2), all the objects involved in Equation~\eqref{eq: Gauss PSL(2,C)} become real, and one recovers precisely the Gauss-Codazzi equations defining immersions in $\mathbb H^3$. 

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  

Finally, let us consider item (3). Since the pull-back metric is assumed to be complex positive (see Definition~\ref{def: positive}), the isotropic directions do not belong to the real tangent space to the surface. Therefore the first fundamental form can never have signature $(1,1)$, i.e. it is necessarily Riemannian. Hence, the unit normal vector field to $\Sigma$ inside $T \mathbb{A}\mathrm{d}\mathbb{S}^3$ is timelike, and coincides with $i \, N$, where $N$ is the unit normal in $T \mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{C})$. This is why the second fundamental form of $\Sigma$ as an immersed surface in $\mathbb{A}\mathrm{d}\mathbb{S}^3$ is equal to $i\, \mathtt {II}$. As we write Equation~\eqref{eq: Gauss PSL(2,C)} in terms of $i \, \mathtt {II}$, we get $\mathrm K_{\mathtt I} =-1 -\mathrm{det}_{\mathtt I}(i \, \mathtt {II})=-1+\mathrm{det}_{\mathtt I}(\mathtt {II})$, yielding the usual equations for the Anti-de Sitter case (see \cite[\S~6.1]{bonsante2020}).
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- defn-9: body_md -->
Let $\sigma\colon \Sigma\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ be a positive  immersion. Then $\sigma$ is \emph{minimal}  if $\trace_{\mathtt I}\mathtt {II}=0$.
<!-- end defn-9 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{thm: II sum of quadratic diffs}
    Let $\mathtt I$ be a positive complex metric on an oriented surface $\Sigma$ and let $(J_1,-J_2)$ be the associated pair of complex structures. Then $\trace_{\mathtt I}\mathtt {II}=0$ and $\nabla^\mathtt I\mathtt {II}$ is tri-symmetric if and only if $\mathtt {II}$ can be expressed as
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: II sum hqd}
        \mathtt {II}=\frac 1 2 q_1+\frac 1 2\overline{q_2}~,
    \end{equation}
    for  $q_1\in \operatorname{\mathrm{QD}}_{J_1}(\Sigma)$ and $\overline{q_2}\in \operatorname{\mathrm{QD}}_{-J_2}(\Sigma)$.
                                                                             
    Moreover,  $q_1$ and $\overline{q_2}$ are unique.
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The proof relies on ideas from \cite{emam2024bers, rungi2024complex}. 
Let $z$ and $\overline w$ be local holomorphic coordinates for the pull-back complex structures of $J_1$ and $-J_2$ on $\Sigma$, respectively. Clearly, $\mathrm{d}z$ and $\mathrm{d}\overline w$ are linearly independent at every point of $\Sigma$, as they have different kernels, corresponding to the two isotropic directions of $\mathtt I$. In particular, $\mathrm{d}z$ and $\mathrm{d}\overline w$ span $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T^*\Sigma$ wherever they are simultaneously defined.

Being $\mathtt {II}$ a $(2,0)$--tensor it can locally be written as 
    \[
    \mathtt {II}= \alpha(z,\overline w)\,\mathrm{d}z^2+ \beta(z,\overline w) \,\mathrm{d}z\mathrm{d}\overline w +\gamma(z,\overline w) \,\mathrm{d}\overline w^2~,
    \]
    for smooth local functions $\alpha,\beta, \gamma$. To prove the statement, we have to show that $\tr_{\mathtt I}\mathtt {II}=0$ and $\nabla^{\mathtt I}\mathtt {II}$ is tri-symmetric if and only if $\alpha $ is $J_1$-holomorphic, $\gamma$ is $(-J_2)$-holomorphic, and $\beta=0$. Let $\mathtt I=\varrho \, \mathrm{d}z\mathrm{d}\overline w$ be the positive metric written in the isotropic local frame $\{\partial_{\overline z},\partial_w\}$, where $\varrho=\varrho(z,\overline w)$ is a smooth, nowhere-vanishing function. Let us define $s^2:=\mathtt I(\partial_{\overline z},\partial_w)=\frac{1}{2}\varrho(\partial_wz)(\partial_{\overline z}\overline w)$ and consider the $\mathtt I$--orthonormal local frame
    $$
    \Big\{e_1:=\frac{1}{s\sqrt 2}(\partial_{\overline z}+\partial_w), e_2:=i\frac{1}{s\sqrt 2}(\partial_{\overline z}-\partial_w)\Big\}~,
    $$
    for a choice of a square root of $\varrho$, possibly in a smaller contractible open subset. Using this frame we can compute
    \begin{align*}
    \trace_{\mathtt I}\mathtt {II} &=\mathtt {II}(e_1,e_1)+\mathtt {II}(e_2,e_2) \\ &=\frac{1}{2s^2}\Big(\mathtt {II}(\partial_{\overline z}+\partial_w,\partial_{\overline z}+\partial_w)-\mathtt {II}(\partial_{\overline z}-\partial_w,\partial_{\overline z}-\partial_w)\Big)\\&=\frac 2 {\mathtt I(\partial_{\overline z}, \partial_w)} \mathtt {II}(\partial_{\overline z}, \partial_w) \\ &=2\varrho^{-1}\beta(z,\overline w)~,
    \end{align*}
    hence $\trace_{\mathtt I}\mathtt {II}=0$ if and only if $\beta=0$. By differentiating $\mathtt {II}$ we get
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: nabla II try simmetric proof}
    \nabla^\mathtt I \mathtt {II}= \mathrm{d}\alpha \otimes \mathrm{d}z^2 + 2\alpha\,(\nabla^\mathtt I \mathrm{d}z)\cdot \mathrm{d}z + \mathrm{d}\gamma \otimes \mathrm{d}\overline w^2+ 2\gamma\,(\nabla^\mathtt I \mathrm{d}\overline w)\cdot \mathrm{d}\overline w~.
    \end{equation}
   We show that $\nabla^{\mathtt I}\mathrm{d}z$ is symmetric. By metric compatibility, we have $\mathtt I(\nabla^{\mathtt I} \partial_{\overline z}, \partial_{\overline z})=\frac 12 \mathrm{d}(\mathtt I(\partial_{\overline z}, \partial_{\overline z}))=0$, hence $\nabla^{\mathtt I} \partial_{\overline z}\in \Gamma(\mathbb{C}T^*S \otimes \mathrm{Span}_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}(\partial_{\overline z}))$ since $\mathtt I$ is nondegenerate. Moreover, the identities
   \[
   (\nabla^{\mathtt I} \mathrm{d}z)(\partial_{\overline z})= \mathrm{d}(\mathrm{d}z(\partial_{\overline z})) - \mathrm{d}z(\nabla^{\mathtt I} \partial_{\overline z}) =0
   \]
    and
    \[
   (\nabla_{\partial_{\overline z}}^\mathtt I \mathrm{d}z)(\partial_{z})= \partial_{\overline z}(1) - \mathrm{d}z(\nabla_{ \partial_{\overline z}}^\mathtt I \partial_z)= -\mathrm{d}z(\nabla_{\partial_z}^\mathtt I { \partial_{\overline z}} ) = 0
   \]
   imply that $\nabla^\mathtt I \mathrm{d}z \in\mathrm{Span}_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}(\mathrm{d}z^2)$. Similarly we observe that $\nabla^\mathtt I \mathrm{d}\overline w\in \mathrm{Span}_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}(\mathrm{d}\overline w^2)$. By Equation~\eqref{eq: nabla II try simmetric proof}, we directly obtain that $\nabla^\mathtt I \mathtt {II}$ is tri-symmetric if and only if $\tau:= \mathrm{d}\alpha \otimes \mathrm{d}z^2 + \mathrm{d}\gamma \otimes \mathrm{d}\overline w^2$ is tri-symmetric. In order to conclude the proof, notice that if $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ are holomorphic for $J_1$ and $-J_2$ respectively, then $\tau= \partial_z\alpha\, \mathrm{d}z^3 + \partial_{\overline w} \gamma \, \mathrm{d}\overline w^3$, which is clearly tri-symmetric. Conversely, if $\tau$ is tri-symmetric, imposing $\tau( \partial_{\overline z}, \partial_z, \partial_w)= \tau(  \partial_z, \partial_{\overline z},\partial_w)$ and $\tau(\partial_{w}, \partial_{\overline w}, \partial_{\overline z})= \tau(\partial_{\overline w},\partial_{w}, \partial_{\overline z})$, we get respectively that $\partial_{\overline z} \alpha=0$ and $\partial_w \gamma=0$, hence $\alpha$ is $J_1$--holomorphic and $\gamma$ is $(-J_2)$--holomorphic.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor: GC semplificato}
    Let $h$ be a positive complex metric of curvature $-1$ on an oriented surface $\Sigma$, whose associated complex structures are $J_1$ and $-J_2$, let $\mathtt {II}$ be a complex $(0,2)$--symmetric tensor of the form $\mathtt {II}=(q_1+\overline{q_2})/2$ for $q_1\in \operatorname{\mathrm{QD}}_{J_1}(\Sigma)$ and $\overline{q_2}\in \operatorname{\mathrm{QD}}_{-J_2}(\Sigma)$, and let $\varrho\colon \Sigma\to \operatorname{\mathbb{C}}^*$ be a smooth function. Then the pair $(\mathtt I:=\varrho h, \mathtt {II})$ satisfies the Equation~\eqref{eq: Gauss PSL(2,C)} if and only if $\varrho$ solves
        \begin{equation}
            \label{eq: Gauss varrho}
            \Delta_{h} \log(\varrho)= 2\varrho + \frac{2q_1\overline{q_2}}{\varrho h^2} -2~.
        \end{equation}
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $z$ and $\overline w$ be local coordinates for $J_1$ and $-J_2$, respectively. Denoting $q_1=\operatorname{\varphi} \mathrm{d}z^2$, $\overline{q_2}= \overline \psi \mathrm{d}\overline w^2$, $h=\lambda \mathrm{d}z \mathrm{d}\overline w$, the tensors $\mathtt I$ and $\mathtt {II}$ are given in the local frame $(\partial_w, \partial_{\overline z})$ by the matrices
\[
\mathtt I \longleftrightarrow \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & \frac 12 \lambda \rho \partial_{\overline z}\overline w \partial_w z \\
    \frac 12 \lambda \rho \partial_{\overline z}\overline w \partial_w z & 0 
\end{pmatrix} \qquad \mathtt {II} \longleftrightarrow
\begin{pmatrix}
    \operatorname{\varphi} (\partial_w z)^2 & 0\\
    0 & \overline{\psi} (\partial_{\overline z} \overline w)^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

    Hence, we compute $${\det}_{\mathtt I}\mathtt {II}= -\frac {\operatorname{\varphi} \overline \psi}{\varrho^2 \lambda^2 }=-\frac{q_1\overline{q_2}}{\varrho^2 h^2}.$$ As a result, through Equation~\eqref{eq: conf curvature}, we deduce that the Gauss equation~\eqref{eq: Gauss PSL(2,C)} is equivalent to Equation~\eqref{eq: Gauss varrho}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{thm: GC semplification 2}
    Let $S$ be a closed oriented surface. Given:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item two complex structures $J_1$ and $J_2$ compatible with the orientation of $S$,
        \item two holomorphic quadratic differentials $q_1\in \operatorname{\mathrm{QD}}_{J_1}(S)$ and $\overline{q_2}\in \operatorname{\mathrm{QD}}_{-J_2}(S)$, and
        \item a smooth function $\varrho:S\to\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}^ *$.
    \end{itemize} 
    there exists an equivariant positive minimal immersion $\sigma\colon\widetilde S\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ with $\mathtt I=\varrho \, \vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}$ and $\mathtt {II}=(q_1+\overline{q_2})/2$ as first and second fundamental form if and only if $\varrho$ solves
    \begin{equation}
            \label{eq: Gauss varrho on S}
            \Delta_{\vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}} \log(\varrho)= 2\varrho + \frac{2q_1\overline{q_2}}{\varrho \, \vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}^2} -2~.
        \end{equation}
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
First, a direct consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm: integration GC} and Remark~\ref{rmk:uniqueness post composition} is that equivariant immersions of $\widetilde{S}$ are uniquely determined (up to post-composition with elements of $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})\times \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$) by pairs $(\mathtt I,\mathtt {II})$ on $S$, solving Equations~\eqref{eq: Gauss PSL(2,C)} and~\eqref{eq: Codazzi PSL(2,C)}. By Theorem~\ref{thm: II sum of quadratic diffs} and Corollary~\ref{cor: GC semplificato}, this is equivalent to pairs of the form $(\mathtt I=\varrho \, \vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)},\mathtt {II}=(q_1+\overline{q_2})/2)$, together with a solution of Equation~\eqref{eq: Gauss varrho} for $h=\vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- defn-10: body_md -->
A positive  minimal immersion $\sigma\colon\widetilde S\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ is called a \emph{regular minimal immersion} if its complex first fundamental form $\mathtt I$ is of the form $\mathtt I=e^{2u}\vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}$.
<!-- end defn-10 -->
<!-- defn-11: body_md -->
Given a regular minimal immersion $\sigma\colon\widetilde S\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$, we denote by $\gamma_\sigma$ the 5-tuple $(J_1,q_1, -J_2, \overline{q_2}, u)$ such that $\mathtt I=e^{2u}\vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}$, $\mathtt {II}=(q_1+\overline{q_2})/2$ and $u$ solves Equation~\eqref{eq: Gauss semplif in u}.
<!-- end defn-11 -->
<!-- defn-12: body_md -->
\label{def:regular immersion}
    A regular minimal immersion $\sigma$ is called \emph{infinitesimally rigid} if $\partial_u\mathscr G$ is bijective at $\gamma_{\sigma}$.
<!-- end defn-12 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop: dense open subset quasi-fuchsian}
    The subset $$\mathcal B_{reg}:=\{(J_1, -J_2)\in \mathcal C(S)\times\mathcal C(\overline S)\  |\ (J_1, 0, -J_2, 0, 0)\in \mathrm M^*(S)\}$$ is open and dense in $\mathcal C(S)\times \mathcal C(\overline S)$. Moreover, the intersection of $\mathcal B_{reg}$ with every fiber $F$ of the projection $\mathcal C(S)\times\mathcal C(\overline S)\to\mathcal T(S)\times \mathcal T(\overline S)$ is connected and dense in $F$.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop: AF e MGH in M*}
  The images of   $\mathrm{AF}(S)$ and $\mathrm{MGH}(S)$ under the inclusions~\eqref{eq:inclusion AF in M} and~\eqref{eq:inclusion MGH in M}, respectively, are contained inside $\mathrm M^*(S)$.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We need to check that, given a 5-tuple of the form $\gamma=(J, q, -J, \pm\overline q, u)$ for $(J,q,u)$ in $\mathrm{AF}(S)$ (resp. $\mathrm{MGH}(S)$), the linearized operator $\partial_u\mathscr G$ is injective.
Observe that, at $\gamma$, $\partial_u\mathscr G$ restricts to a linear operator $L\colon C^{\infty}(S,\mathbb R)\to C^{\infty}(S,\mathbb R)$, and, by $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$--linearity, $\partial_u\mathscr G$ is injective if and only if $L$ is injective. 


By Equation~\eqref{eq: linearized Gauss}, we have
\[
L(v)=\partial_u \mathscr G (v)= \Delta_{h_J} v -2e^{2u}\left(1\pm \frac{|q|^2}{e^{4u}h_J^2} \right)  v~,
\]
for $v\in C^{\infty}(S,\mathbb R)$, where $h_J=\vb*h(J,-J)$.
The sign is negative for the case of $\mathrm{AF}(S)$ and positive for the case of $\mathrm{MGH}(S)$. In either case (recall that in the former case we assume $e^{-4u}|q|^2/h_J^2<1$), we deduce:
\[
\int_S v L(v) \, \mathrm{d}A_h \leq  \int_S  v (\Delta_{h_J} v)  \,\mathrm{d}A_h = - \int_S \|\nabla^{h_J} v\|^2 \,\mathrm{d}A_h \le 0~,
\]
with equality if and only if $v$ is identically zero. This concludes the argument for the injectivity of $L$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop: Frechet structure}
$\mathrm{M}^*(S)$ is a complex Fréchet submanifold of $\mathrm{QD}(S)\times \mathrm{QD}(\overline S) \times C^{\infty}(S,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ and the projection $\pi_0:\mathrm{M}^*(S)\to \operatorname{\mathrm{QD}}(S)\times\operatorname{\mathrm{QD}}(\overline S)$ is a local biholomorphism.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The projection map $\pi_0\colon \mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathrm{QD}(S)\times \mathrm{QD}(\overline S)$, according to Proposition~\ref{prop: Frechet structure}, is a local biholomorphism and is clearly equivariant for the (diagonal) action of $\mathrm{Diff}_0(S)$. 
Observe that this implies that the space $\mathrm M^*(S)/\mathrm{Diff}_0(S)$ is not finite dimensional. As a consequence, one can find uncountably many regular minimal surfaces in $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ with the same holonomy. 
Nevertheless, we will now explain how to construct (using a similar process as in \cite[\S~6.1]{ESrank2}) a meaningful finite dimensional quotient of $\mathrm M^*(S)$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- defn-13: body_md -->
\label{def:M(S)}
    We define $\mathbb{M}(S)$ as the topological quotient of $\mathrm M^*(S)$ obtained by contracting to points the connected components of the fibers of $[\pi_0]$. We will denote by $\mathbb{M}_0(S)$ the connected component of $\mathbb M(S)$ containing the elements $[(J,0,-J,0 ,0)]$, which parametrize an isomorphic copy of Teichm\"uller space inside $\mathbb M(S)$.
<!-- end defn-13 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{thm: Kernel projection equal to Lie derivatives}
    The space $\mathbb M(S)$ has a structure of complex manifold for which the quotient map $\mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathbb M(S)$ is holomorphic, and the natural projection $\pi\colon \mathbb M(S)\to \mathbb{QD}(S) \times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S) $ is a local biholomorphism.
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{prop: TSTS dentro mathbb M}
   Consider the space $\mathcal B_{reg}$ defined in Proposition~\ref{prop: dense open subset quasi-fuchsian}. The inclusion 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: Breg dentro M*}
        \begin{split}
                \mathcal B_{reg} &\hookrightarrow \mathrm M^*(S)\\
        (J_1, -{J_2})&\mapsto (J_1, 0, -{J_2}, 0, 0)
        \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    descends to a well-defined proper holomorphic embedding 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eq: TSTS in mathbb M}
            \mathcal T(S)\times \mathcal T(\overline S)\hookrightarrow \mathbb M_0(S)
    \end{equation}
    given by $[(J_1, -{J_2})]\mapsto[(J_1, 0, -{J_2}, 0, 0)]$.
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Fix $F$ a fiber of the projection $\mathcal C(S)\times \mathcal C(\overline S)\to \mathcal T(S)\times \mathcal T(\overline S)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop: dense open subset quasi-fuchsian}, the intersection $F\cap \mathcal B_{reg}$ is non-empty and connected, hence 
    \[
    \{  (J_1, 0, -{J_2}, 0, 0) \in \mathrm M^*(S) \ |\ (J_1, -J_2)\in F\cap \mathcal B_{reg}\} 
    \]
    is connected. By the construction of $\mathbb M(S)$, the image of this subset via the projection $\mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathbb M(S)$ is just the point $\{ [ (J_1, 0, -{J_2}, 0, 0) ]\} $, which is therefore the same for all $(J_1, -J_2)\in F\cap \mathcal B_{reg}$. This proves that the map~\eqref{eq: TSTS in mathbb M} is well-defined.

To see that it is holomorphic, observe that the map in Equation~\eqref{eq: Breg dentro M*} is trivially holomorphic, hence Equation~\eqref{eq: TSTS in mathbb M} is holomorphic as it can be locally seen as the composition of holomorphic local inverses of $\mathcal B_{reg}\to \mathcal T(S)\times \mathcal T(\overline S)$ with the map~\eqref{eq: Breg dentro M*}, and the projection $\mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathbb M(S)$.
    
    Finally, the map~\eqref{eq: TSTS in mathbb M} is an inverse of the submersion $\mathbb M(S)\to \mathcal T(S)\times \mathcal T(\overline S)$ on the first and third factor, hence it is a proper embedding.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{prop: AF and MGH are totally real submanifolds}
  The inclusions $\mathrm{AF}(S)\subset \mathrm M^*(S)$ and $\mathrm{MGH}(S)\subset \mathrm M^*(S)$ descend to totally real full dimensional embeddings of $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ into $\mathbb M_0(S)$.
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
We show it for $\mathcal{AF}(S)$, and the proof for $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ follows in the same fashion. As we discussed in Proposition~\ref{prop: AF e MGH in M*}, the space of almost-Fuchsian minimal immersions corresponds to the subset of $\mathrm M^*(S)$ given by $\mathrm{AF}(S)$. On this subspace, the fibers of the projection $[\pi_0]$ to $\mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)$ correspond to the orbits of the (diagonal) action of $\mathrm{Diff}_0(S)$, hence they are connected. As a result, this inclusion descends to a continuous injective map $\mathcal{AF}(S)\hookrightarrow\mathbb M_0(S)$. To check that it is a smooth totally real immersion (see Definition~\ref{def: totally real submanifold}), it is sufficient to observe that, on local charts on which $\pi\colon \mathbb M_0(S)\to \mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)$ restricts to a biholomorphism, the inclusion of $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ into  $\mathbb M_0(S)$ corresponds to the inclusion of $\mathbb{QD}(S)$ given by $[J,q]\mapsto ([J,q],[-J, \overline q])$, whose image is easily checked to be totally real. Finally, to see that this inclusion is an embedding, observe that the map $[J,q]\mapsto [(J,q,-J, \overline q, u)]$ allows to see $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ as the image of a section, defined on an open subset of $\mathbb{QD}(S)$, of the submersion 
    $$
    \mathbb M_0(S)\xrightarrow{\pi} \mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)\xrightarrow{pr_1} \mathbb{QD}(S)~,
    $$
    where $pr_1$ is the projection on the first factor: as a consequence, $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb M_0(S)$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rmk: restriction of pi on AF and MGH}
Consider the natural projections $\pi_{\mathcal{AF}}\colon \mathcal {AF}(S)\to \mathbb{QD}(S)$ and $\pi_{\mathcal{MGH}}\colon \mathcal{MGH}(S)\to \mathbb{QD}(S)$ given by $[J, q,u]\mapsto [J,q]$. The first one is an embedding onto a \emph{proper} open subset of $\mathbb{QD}(S)$ (see again \cite{uhlenbeck1983}, or the more recent work \cite{bronstein-smith2024} which also provides finer information on the image) while the second one is a diffeomorphism (\cite[Theorem 3.8]{kirill07}). The restrictions of $\pi$ to $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ essentially coincides with $\pi_{\mathcal{AF}}$ and $\pi_{\mathcal{MGH}}$, in the sense that \begin{equation}
    \begin{split}
        \pi([J,q, -J ,\overline q, u]) &= ([J,q], [-J, \overline q])= \Big(\pi_{\mathcal{AF}} ([J,q,u]),\overline{\pi_{\mathcal{AF}} ([J,q,u])}
        \Big)~, \\
         \pi([J,q, -J ,-\overline q, u]) &= ([J,q], [-J, -\overline q])= \Big(\pi_{\mathcal{MGH}} ([J,q,u]),\overline{\pi_{\mathcal{MGH}} ([J,-q,u])}\Big)~. 
\end{split}
   \end{equation}
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
\label{thm: boman}
    A map between Fréchet spaces is smooth if and only if it maps $C^{\infty}$--curves to $C^{\infty}$--curves.
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{prop: holo smooth dependence}
    Let $\Lambda$ be a smooth (resp. complex) manifold, and let  ${(\mathtt I_{\lambda}, \mathtt {II}_{\lambda})}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ be a family of equivariant immersion data of $\widetilde S$ into $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ whose holonomy representations are in $\chi^{*}\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)$.
    
    Assume that, at each point $p\in S$, the maps $\mathtt I_{\cdot}|_p,\mathtt {II}_{\cdot}|_p\colon \Lambda\to \mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T_p S)$ are smooth (resp. holomorphic) in $\lambda \in \Lambda$. Then there exists a map
   \[
        \sigma: \Lambda \times \widetilde S\longrightarrow \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})
    \]
    such that $\sigma(\lambda, \cdot) \colon \widetilde S\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ is an equivariant immersion with immersion data $(\mathtt I_{\lambda}, \mathtt {II}_{\lambda})$, and such that $\sigma(\cdot, p)\colon \Lambda\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ is smooth (resp. holomorphic) for every $p\in \widetilde S$.
   
    If the metrics $\mathtt I_{\lambda}$ are positive, and the holonomy map
    \begin{align*} &\Lambda\longrightarrow\chi\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big) \\ &\lambda \longmapsto {hol}(\sigma_\lambda)
    \end{align*}
has image in $\chi^*\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)$, then this map is smooth (resp. holomorphic).
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The original result from Bonsante-El Emam \cite{BEE} is stated only in the holomorphic category. However, the proof argument from \cite{BEE} can also be applied to deduce the result in the smooth setting. Indeed, if we assume that the family ${(\mathtt I_{\lambda}, \mathtt {II}_{\lambda})}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ depends smoothly on $\lambda$, Proposition~5.5 in \cite{BEE} implies that there exists a smooth map $\Phi\colon \Lambda\times \widetilde S\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{C})^2$ such that the evaluation map of $\Phi$ at any point of $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ gives a smooth map $\sigma\colon \Lambda\times \widetilde S\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop: holo smooth dependence}. 
    To see the part of the statement involving the holonomy, observe first of all that $\sigma_{\lambda}$ is invariant for at most one homomorphism $\rho_{\lambda}\colon \pi_1(S)\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2$ by Remark \ref{rmk:uniqueness post composition}. More precisely, for all $\gamma\in \pi_1(S)$, $\rho_{\lambda}$ is characterized by the conditions $\sigma_{\lambda}\circ \gamma=  \rho_{\lambda}(\gamma)\circ \sigma_{\lambda}$ and $N_{\sigma_{\lambda}\circ \lambda} = d( \rho_{\lambda}(\gamma)) (N_{\sigma_{\lambda}})$, where $N_{\sigma_{\lambda}}$ is the unit normal of $\sigma_{\lambda}$. These conditions allow to see that the map $\lambda\mapsto \rho_{\lambda}(\gamma)$ is smooth and compute its derivatives explicitly.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rmk: pointwise holo and global holo}
The pointwise smoothness/holomorphicity condition assumed in Proposition~\ref{prop: holo smooth dependence} is equivalent to requiring that the maps $\Lambda\to \Gamma(\mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS))$ given by $\lambda \mapsto \mathtt I_\lambda$ and $\lambda \mapsto \mathtt {II}_{\lambda}$ are smooth/holomorphic as maps between Fréchet manifolds. Indeed, as shown in \cite[Theorem~I.3.12]{kriegl1997convenient},                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                  
we have the identification 
\begin{align*}
C^{\infty}(\Lambda, C^{\infty}(S,  \mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)))& \cong C^{\infty}(\Lambda\times S, \mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS))\\
\left(\lambda\mapsto \alpha_{\lambda}\right) &\mapsto   \left((\lambda,p)\mapsto \alpha_{\lambda}(p)\right)~.
\end{align*}
Also, the holomorphicity conditions are trivially equivalent by the identification between the differential maps of the two formats.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem: from M* to I II}
    The map
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eq: from M* to I II}
    \begin{split}
        \mathrm M^*(S)&\to \Gamma(\mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS))^2\\
        \gamma= (J_1, q_1, -J_2, \overline{q_2}, u) &\mapsto (\mathtt I_{\gamma}, \mathtt {II}_{\gamma}):= (e^{2u}\vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}, q_1+\overline{q_2})~,
    \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    is holomorphic.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop: Bers metrics holo dependence}, the map $(J_1, -J_2) \mapsto \vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}$ is holomorphic. Therefore, the function $\gamma\mapsto (\mathtt I_{\gamma}, \mathtt {II}_{\gamma})$ is holomorphic as it is the restriction of the following holomorphic map:
     \begin{gather*}
     \mathcal C(S)\times \Gamma(\mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS))\times \mathcal C(\overline S) \times \Gamma(\mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS))\times C^{\infty}(S,\mathbb C)\to (\Gamma(\mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS))^2 , \\
     (J_1, \alpha, -J_2, \beta, u) \mapsto (e^{2u}\vb*h{(J_1, -J_2)}, \alpha+\beta) .
     \end{gather*}
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem: holo dependence}
        Let $\Lambda$ be a smooth (resp. complex) manifold and let $F:\Lambda\to \mathrm M^*(S)$ be a smooth (resp. holomorphic) map. Then the composition $\mathrm{hol}\circ F:\Lambda \to  \chi^{*}\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)$ is smooth (resp. holomorphic).
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The composition of $F$ with the map from Equation~\eqref{eq: from M* to I II} is a smooth/holomorphic map $\Lambda\to (\Gamma(\mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)))^2$, by Lemma~\ref{lem: from M* to I II}. By Remark~\ref{rmk: pointwise holo and global holo}, the composed map is smooth/holomorphic pointwise, hence it gives a family $\lambda\mapsto (\mathtt I_{\lambda}, \mathtt {II}_{\lambda})$ as in the hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{prop: holo smooth dependence}. The lemma then follows by Proposition~\ref{prop: holo smooth dependence}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- thm-9: body_md -->
\label{thm: hol su M^* is holomorphic}
 The holonomy map ${hol}\colon \mathrm M^*(S)\to \chi^*(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2)$ is holomorphic.
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem: holo dependence}, $\mathrm{hol}$ maps $C^{\infty}$--curves into $C^{\infty}$--curves and, hence, it is smooth by Theorem~\ref{thm: boman}. 
    
    To see that the map is holomorphic, we fix $\sigma\in \mathrm M^*(S)$ and $\dot \sigma \in T_{\sigma}\mathrm M^*(S)$. Then, by taking a local chart, we can find a (small) complex submanifold $L$ of $\mathrm M^*(S)$ of complex dimension $1$ passing through $\sigma$ and such that $T_{\sigma}L=\mathrm{Span}_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}(\dot \sigma)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem: holo dependence}, the restriction of $\mathrm{hol}$ to $L$ is holomorphic and, hence, $\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{hol})_{\sigma}(i \, \dot \sigma) = i \, \mathrm{d}(\mathrm{hol})_{\sigma}(\dot \sigma)$. We conclude that $\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{hol})_{\sigma}$ is $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$--linear for all $\sigma\in \mathrm M^*(S)$. Thus, $\mathrm{hol}$ is holomorphic.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
The complex Lie derivative of a complex structure was originally defined in \cite{emam2024bers} in a slightly different way. The discussion above shows that the definition in \cite{emam2024bers} of complex Lie derivative of $J$ is equal to the $(1,0)$--part of the one considered here. In particular, since in this paper we will mostly work with the holomorphic tangent bundle of the space of complex structures (and of holomorphic quadratic differentials) the two notions actually coincide and we will remove the superscript $(1,0)$ from the notation.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- prop-11: body_md -->
\label{prop: tangent fiber M*}
     For all $\gamma\in \mathrm M^*(S)$, an element $X\in T^{1,0}_{\gamma}\mathrm M^*(S)$ lies in the kernel of the differential of $\mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathbb M(S)$ at $\gamma$ if and only if it is of the form 
     $\mathscr L_X\gamma$ for some $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$, where $\mathscr L_X\gamma$ denotes the complex Lie derivative $\mathscr L_X$ on each entry of the 5-tuple $\gamma$.
<!-- end prop-11 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem: invariance of map under Diff-action}
Let $\mathbb X$ be a complex manifold and let $\hat F:\mathrm M^*(S)\to\mathbb X$ be a holomorphic map. Then $\hat F$ descends to a well-defined holomorphic map $F:\mathbb M(S)\to\mathbb X$ if and only if $\hat F$ is invariant under the action of $\operatorname{Diff}_0(S)$ on $\mathrm M^*(S)$.  Equivalently, $F$ descends to $\hat F$ if and only if $\mathrm d\hat F\big(\mathscr L_{\mathsf X}\gamma)=0$ for all $\mathsf X\in \Gamma(TS)$ and $\gamma\in\mathrm{M}^*(S)$.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- thm-10: body_md -->
\label{thm: hol from mathbb M is holo}
    The holonomy map ${hol}: \mathrm M^*(S)\to \chi^*\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)$ descends to a well-defined holomorphic function $\mathrm{hol}: \mathbb M(S)\to \chi^*\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)$.
<!-- end thm-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The map $hol$ is holomorphic by Theorem~\ref{thm: hol su M^* is holomorphic}, and it is clearly $\mathrm{Diff}_0(S)$-invariant. The statement now follows from Lemma~\ref{lem: invariance of map under Diff-action}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
Most of the statements in this section also appear in \cite{ESrank2} in the setting of complex harmonic $ G$--bundles for $ G=\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)\times \mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)$, corresponding to complex harmonic maps into $\mathbb G\times \mathbb G$. In fact, the two approaches produce the same space $\mathrm M^*(S)$ of immersion data, hence the same quotient $\mathbb M(S)$, despite they parametrize immersions in different spaces. Since the data have a different geometric meaning, the holonomy maps from $\mathrm M^*(S)$ and $\mathbb M(S)$ defined in the two papers could be different a priori, therefore we had to prove independently that the holonomy maps defined in this paper are holomorphic. Observe that, a posteriori, the holonomy maps in the two papers coincide on $\mathbb M_0(S)$, as the two holomorphic maps coincide on the totally real locus $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$: indeed, the correspondence between minimal immersions into $\mathbb{A}\mathrm{d}\mathbb{S}^3$ and $G$-Hitchin Higgs bundles corresponding to a pair of quadratic differentials $(q,-q)$ is obtained explicitly via the the non-abelian Hodge correspondence and the Gauss map on $\mathbb{A}\mathrm{d}\mathbb{S}^3$.  
    
    In fact, we believe that the two holonomy maps coincide on $\mathrm M^*(S)$ via an analogue approach using the Gauss map, even if attention should be paid to the relation with the complex harmonic Higgs bundles setting treated in \cite{ESrank2}. Since these aspects are beyond the scope of this paper, we defer further clarification to some future work of the first author and Sagman.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- thm-11: body_md -->
\label{thm: hol local biholo}
    The holonomy map $\mathrm{hol}:\mathbb M(S)\to \chi^{*}\big(\pi_1(S), \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)$ is a local biholomorphism.
<!-- end thm-11 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
\label{prop: trivial sigma variation gives trivial gamma variation}
    Let $\sigma_t\colon \widetilde S\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ be a smooth path of regular minimal immersions with immersion data $\gamma_t$. If $\dot \sigma=\mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X)$ for some $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$, then $\dot\gamma=\mathscr L_X\gamma$.
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem: mappa I II olomorfa}
The map 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq: mappa I, II di sigma}
\begin{split}
(\mathtt I,\mathtt {II})\colon \mathscr U &\to \Gamma(\mathrm{Sym}_2(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS))^2 \\
\sigma&\mapsto (\mathtt I_{\sigma}, \mathtt {II}_{\sigma})
\end{split}
\end{equation}
is holomorphic.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Denote by $ \mathtt b $ the Killing form on $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$. 
For $\sigma\in \mathscr U$, denote by $N_{\sigma}$ a unit normal vector field. Let $v\in \operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T_xS$ be any vector such that $\mathtt I_{\sigma}(v,v)\ne 0$, so that the triple $(v, \mathcal Jv, N_{\sigma})$ is an orthogonal basis of $T_{\sigma(x)}\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$. Let $\dot \sigma\in T_{\sigma}\mathscr U$ and denote by $\dot \mathtt I_\sigma$ and $\dot \mathtt {II}_\sigma$ the infinitesimal variations of the first and the second fundamental form, respectively, as defined in the statement. 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
By definition of the metric on $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$, we have that, for all $w\in \operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T\widetilde S$
\begin{equation}\label{eq: metrica complessa positiva in Lemma}
\mathtt I_{\sigma}(w,w)=\mathtt b \left(L_{\sigma(x)}^* \left(\mathrm{d}\sigma(w)\right), L_{\sigma(x)}^* \left(\mathrm{d}\sigma(w)\right)\right).
\end{equation}

It follows that a smooth curve $\sigma_t$ in $\mathscr U$ determines a family of  tensors $\mathtt I_{\sigma_t}$ that depend smoothly on $t$.
Similarly, $\mathcal J_{\sigma}(v)$ is characterized by the following equations:
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eq: bicomplessa in Lemma}
    \begin{aligned}
        &\mathtt I_{\sigma}(\mathcal J_{\sigma}(v),\mathcal J_{\sigma}(v))=\mathtt I_{\sigma}(v,v),\\
        & \mathtt I_{\sigma}(\mathcal J_{\sigma}(v),v)=0.\end{aligned}\end{equation}
        
We observe that, since $v$ and   $\mathcal J_{\sigma}(v)$      form a basis of $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS$ whenever $v\neq 0$, if equations~\eqref{eq: metrica complessa positiva in Lemma} hold for some $v\neq 0$, then they hold for every $v$. 
        As before, a smooth curve $\sigma_t$ in $\mathscr U$ determines smoothly varying tensors $\mathcal J_{\sigma_t}$. 
 We may also repeat the same argument to show that $N_{\sigma_t}$ and, finally, $\mathtt {II}_{\sigma_t}$ depend smoothly on $t$ if $\sigma_t$ does, by observing that $N_{\sigma_t}$ is uniquely determined by:
    
  \begin{equation}
  \label{eq: normale in Lemma}
      \begin{aligned}
    &\mathtt b\left(L_{\sigma}^* \left(\mathrm{d}\sigma(v)\right), L_{\sigma}^* N_{\sigma}\right)=0\\
    &\mathtt b \left(L_{\sigma}^*\left( \mathrm{d}\sigma(J_{\sigma} v)\right),  L_{\sigma}^*N_{\sigma}\right) =0\\
    &\mathtt b \left(L_{\sigma}^*N_{\sigma} ,  L_{\sigma}^*N_{\sigma}\right) =1, 
\end{aligned}
 \end{equation}
while $\mathtt {II}_{\sigma_t}$ is defined as:

     \begin{equation}\label{eq: II in Lemma}\begin{aligned}                                                                                                                                                            
        \mathtt {II}_{\sigma}(w,v) &=  -\mathtt I_{\sigma} \left(w, \sigma^*\left(D_{\mathrm{d}\sigma(v)} N_{\sigma}\right)\right)  \\ 
        &=\mathtt b \left( L_{\sigma(x)}^*\left(\mathrm{d}\sigma(v) \right),L_{\sigma(x)}^*\left(D_{\mathrm{d}\sigma(v)} N_{\sigma}\right)\right).
    \end{aligned}\end{equation}
       
So, by the Generalized Boman's Theorem (see Theorem~\ref{thm: boman}), the map~\eqref{eq: mappa I, II di sigma} is $C^{\infty}$.

       
       Moreover, a direct computation by differentiating the equations~\eqref{eq: metrica complessa positiva in Lemma},~\eqref{eq: bicomplessa in Lemma},~\eqref{eq: normale in Lemma} and~\eqref{eq: II in Lemma}, an infinitesimal variation in the direction $i\dot \sigma$ produces the infinitesimal variations $i\dot \mathtt I$, $i\dot{\mathcal J}_{\sigma}$, $i \dot N_{\sigma}$, $i\dot \mathtt {II}$.  Hence the differential of the map~\eqref{eq: mappa I, II di sigma} is $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$--linear, and we therefore conclude that it is also holomorphic.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{lem: complex tangential deformations}
Let $\sigma\in \mathscr U$, and assume that $\dot \sigma\in T_{\sigma}\mathscr U$ is such that $\dot \sigma= \mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X)$, for some $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$. Then the corresponding infinitesimal variations of the first and second fundamental forms are given by $$\dot \mathtt I_\sigma= \mathscr L_X \mathtt I_\sigma , \quad \quad \dot \mathtt {II}_\sigma= \mathscr L_{X} \mathtt {II}_\sigma.$$
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $\mathrm X\in \Gamma(TS)$ and let $\phi_{t\widetilde{\mathrm X}}$ denote the lift to the universal cover of the corresponding flow. Then, $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}|_{t=0} ( \sigma\circ \phi_{t\widetilde{\mathrm X}}) = \mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde{\mathrm X})\in \Gamma(\sigma^* T\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}))$. In particular, we can think of $\mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde{\mathrm X})$ as an element of $T_{\sigma}\mathscr U$. By the properties of the (real) Lie derivative, this infinitesimal deformation determines an infinitesimal variation of $\mathtt I_\sigma$ and $\mathtt {II}_\sigma$ according to the Lie derivative through $\mathrm X$. By Lemma~\ref{lem: mappa I II olomorfa}, for all $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$
  \begin{align*}
  \mathrm{d}(\mathtt I, \mathtt {II})(\mathrm{d}\sigma(X))&=  \mathrm{d}(\mathtt I, \mathtt {II})(\mathrm{d}\sigma(Re(X)))+i \, \mathrm{d}(\mathtt I, \mathtt {II})(\mathrm{d}\sigma(Im(X))) \\
  &=(\mathscr L_{Re(X)}\mathtt I, \mathscr L_{Re(X)}\mathtt {II}) +i \, (\mathscr L_{Im(X)}\mathtt I, \mathscr L_{Im(X)}\mathtt {II})\\& =(\mathscr L_{X}\mathtt I, \mathscr L_{X}\mathtt {II})
  \end{align*}
as claimed.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{lem: map from M* to I and II}
    The map introduced in Equation~\eqref{eq: from M* to I II} has injective differential. Moreover, its differential at $\gamma$ maps $\mathscr L_X \gamma$ to $(\mathscr L_X\mathtt I_{\gamma}, \mathscr L_X{\mathtt {II}}_\gamma)$ for all $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$.
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
We start by proving that the differential map is injective. Consider a path $\gamma^t=(J_1^t, q_1^t, -J_2^t, \overline q_2^t, u^t)\in \mathrm M^*(S)$, let $\mathtt I_t$ and $\mathtt {II}_t$ be the image path and assume that both derivatives $\dot \mathtt I, \dot \mathtt {II}$ vanish at $t = 0$. Let $z_t$ and $\overline {w_t}$ be a path of local coordinates for $J_1^t$ and $-J_2^t$, respectively. Also denote by $\mathcal J_t$ the path of bi-complex structures induced by $(J_1^t,-J_2^t)$. 
 
 We show that the derivative $\dot{\mathcal J}$ of $\mathcal J_t$ at time zero is such that $\dot{\mathcal J}=0$. The condition $\mathcal J_t^2=- id$ implies $\mathcal J\dot{\mathcal J}+\dot{\mathcal J}\mathcal J=0$, from which we see that $\dot {\mathcal J}$ maps the $i$--eigenspace to the $(-i)$ eigenspace and vice versa: equivalently, $\dot{\mathcal J}(\partial_{\overline z})
 \in \mathrm{Span}(\partial_{w})$ and $\dot{\mathcal J}(\partial_{w})\in \mathrm{Span}(\partial_{ \overline z})$. On the other hand, from $\mathtt I_t= \varrho_t \mathrm{d}z_t\mathrm{d}\overline {w_t}$, 
 we get $\mathtt I_t(\mathcal J_t\cdot, \cdot)+\mathtt I_t(\cdot, \mathcal J_t\cdot)=0$, hence $\dot \mathtt I=0$ implies:  $$\mathtt I( \dot {\mathcal J}\cdot, \cdot)+\mathtt I(\cdot, \dot{\mathcal J})=0.$$ By evaluating the left-hand side in $(\partial_{\overline z}, \partial_{\overline z})$, we have that $\mathtt I(\dot {\mathcal J}(\partial_{\overline z}), 
 \partial_{\overline z})=0$: using that $\dot {\mathcal J}(\partial_{\overline z})\in Span(\partial_ w)$, $\mathtt I(\partial_{\overline z}, \partial_{\overline z})=0$, and that $\mathtt I$ is non-degenerate, we 
 conclude that $\dot{\mathcal J}(\partial_{\overline z})=0$. In the same fashion, $\dot{\mathcal J}(\partial_{ w})=0$, hence $\dot{\mathcal J}=0$.

Now, observe that, for any function $v$ we can write
 \[
 \mathrm{d}v=\frac{\partial_w v}{\partial_w z} \mathrm{d}z +\frac{\partial_{\overline z} v}{\partial_{\overline z} \overline w} \mathrm{d}\overline w, \] 
 as one can easily see by evaluating both sides in the basis $\{\partial_{\overline z}, \partial_w\}$. Hence,
$\mathrm{d}v\circ \mathcal J= i \mathrm{d}v$ (resp. $\mathrm{d}v\circ \mathcal J= -i \mathrm{d}v$) if and only if $v$ is holomorphic for  $J_1$ (resp. $-J_2$).
 
 By differentiating the expressions $\mathrm{d}z_t\circ \mathcal J_t= i \mathrm{d}z_t$ and $\mathrm{d}\overline w_t\circ \mathcal J_t= -i\mathrm{d}\overline w_t$ at $t=0$, we get that
 \begin{equation}
     \label{eq: infinitesimal dz and dw}
     \mathrm{d}\dot z\circ \mathcal J= i\mathrm{d}\dot z\qquad \mathrm{d}\dot{\overline w}\circ \mathcal J=-i \mathrm{d}\dot{\overline w}.
 \end{equation}
 We therefore conclude that $\dot z$ is $J_1$--holomorphic, hence the corresponding Beltrami differential is zero, implying that $\dot {c}_1=0$. In the same spirit, we get that $\dot{\overline w}$ is $(-J_2)$--holomorphic and $\dot{\overline {J_2}}=0$. 

 Since $\dot z$ and $\dot{\overline w}$ are holomorphic for $J_1$ and $-J_2$ respectively, $\dot q_1$ and $\dot{ \overline{q_2}}$ are multiples of $\mathrm{d}z^2$ and $\mathrm{d}\overline w^2$ respectively, hence $0=\dot \mathtt {II}=\dot q_1+\dot{ \overline{q_2}}$ implies that $\dot q_1=0=\dot{ \overline{q_2}}$.

Finally, since the projection map $\mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathrm{QD}(S)\times\mathrm{QD}(\overline S)$ has injective differential, we conclude that $\dot \gamma=0$.

To prove the second part of the statement, observe that the map defined in Equation~\eqref{eq: from M* to I II} is clearly equivariant for the action of $\mathrm{Diff}_0(S)$, hence its derivative maps $\mathscr L_{\mathsf X}\gamma$ to $(\mathscr L_{\mathsf X} \mathtt I_{\gamma}, \mathscr L_{\mathsf X} \mathtt {II}_{\gamma} )$ for all $\mathsf X\in \Gamma(TS)$. For $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$, we get the analogue result by writing $\mathscr L_X= \mathscr L_{\Re(X)}+ i\mathscr L_{\Im(X)}$ and using that the differential map is $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$--linear.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem: complex tangential deformations}, the fundamental forms vary infinitesimally according to $\dot \mathtt I=\mathscr L_X \mathtt I$ and $\dot \mathtt {II}=\mathscr L_X\mathtt {II}$. 
Since the differential map of $\gamma\mapsto (\mathtt I_{\gamma}, \mathtt {II}_{\gamma})$ is injective and sends $\dot \gamma$ into $(\mathscr L_X \mathtt I, \mathscr L_X\mathtt {II})$, we conclude that $\dot \gamma=\mathscr L_X\gamma$ thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem: map from M* to I and II}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
\label{prop: minimal deformations with trivial holonomy }
  Consider the map
 \begin{align*}   
 \mathcal R: \ &\mathscr U \to \mathrm{Hom}^*\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)\times C^{\infty}(S,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}) \\ & \ \ \sigma\longmapsto \ \ \big(\rho, H_\sigma\big) \end{align*}
 where $\rho=\mathrm{hol}(\sigma)$ is the holonomy of the immersion and $H_\sigma$ is the function on $S$ whose lift to $\widetilde S$ is the mean curvature $\mathrm{\tr}_{\mathtt I_\sigma}(\mathtt {II}_\sigma)$ of $\sigma$. 
 
 If $\sigma$ is an equivariant regular minimal immersion that is infinitesimally rigid (or, equivalently, if $\gamma_\sigma \in \mathrm{M}^*(S)$), then $\mathrm{d}\mathcal R_{\sigma} (\dot \sigma)=(0,0)$ if and only if $\dot \sigma=\mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X)$ for some $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$.
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $\sigma: \widetilde{S} \to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ be an equivariant, regular minimal immersion. We first prove that $\mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X)$ is tangent to $\mathscr U$ and that $\mathrm{d}\mathcal R(\mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde  X))=(0,0)$ for every $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$. Observe that $\mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X)$ is the derivative at time $t = 0$ of the path of immersions $\sigma_t\in \mathscr U$ given by $\sigma_t (p)= \exp_{\sigma(p)} (t\,\mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X))$ (for sufficiently small values of $|t|$). Since $\mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X)$ is $\rho$--invariant, the maps $\sigma_t : \widetilde{S} \to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ are equivariant with respect to the same representation $\rho$, independently of $t$. Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{lem: complex tangential deformations} and the properties of the Lie derivative, the infinitesimal deformation of the mean curvature along $\dot \sigma$ is given by 
$$
\left. \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \right|_{t=0} \widetilde H_\sigma =\mathscr L_{X}(\mathrm{tr}_{\mathtt I}\mathtt {II})= \mathscr L_X (H_\sigma)~,
$$
which equals zero since $\sigma$ is minimal. Hence, we conclude that $\mathrm{d}\mathcal R_{\sigma} \big( \mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X)\big)=(0,0)$ for all $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$.


We now suppose that $\sigma$ is infinitesimally rigid and show that the kernel of $\mathrm{d}\mathcal R_{\sigma}$ consists only of elements of the form $\mathrm{d}\sigma(X)$. 
So, assume $\dot \sigma\in T_{\sigma}\mathscr U $ is such that $\mathrm{d}\mathcal R_{\sigma}(\dot\sigma)=(0,0)$. By Equation~\eqref{eq: dot sigma e dot rho}, we see that $\dot \sigma$ is a $\rho$--invariant section of $\sigma^*T\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$, or equivalently a $\rho$--invariant vector field on $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ along $\sigma$. Denoting by $N$ the normal vector field along $\sigma$ (which is also $\rho$--equivariant), we can write $\dot \sigma= \mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X)+ \widetilde fN$ for some $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$ and some  complex function $f\colon  S\to \operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$. 

Clearly $\widetilde fN\in T_{\sigma}\mathscr U$, since it is the derivative of the path of immersions $\sigma_t=\exp_{\sigma(p)} (t \widetilde fN)$ for $|t|$ small enough. Moreover, by linearity, we get that
\[
\mathrm{d}\mathcal R_{\sigma}(\widetilde f N)= - \mathrm{d}\mathcal R_{\sigma}(\mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X)) = (0,0)~,
\] 
where the last equality holds by the first part of the argument. It remains to show that $\mathrm{d}\mathcal{R}_{\sigma} (\widetilde fN)=(0,0)$ if and only if $f=0$. 

In Appendix~\ref{appendix:inf mean curv} (see in particular Equation~\eqref{eq:linearized H on S}), we show that the $t$-derivative of $H_{\sigma_t}$ at $t=0$ has the following expression, that holds on the closed surface $S$ since all quantities of interest are $\pi_1(S)$-invariant:
$$
\left. \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \right|_{t=0} H_\sigma = e^{-2u}\partial_u \mathscr G (f)~,
$$
where we recall that the expression for $\partial_u \mathscr G$ has been given in~\eqref{eq: linearized Gauss}. By definition of infinitesimal rigidity, $\partial_u\mathscr G$ is bijective as a linear map from $C^{\infty}(S,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ to itself, and $\dot H_\sigma=0$ by assumption, so we conclude that $f=0$. This concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
We already know that $\mathrm{hol}$ is a holomorphic map by Theorem~\ref{thm: hol from mathbb M is holo}. Therefore, $\mathrm{hol}$ is a local biholomorphism if and only its differential is injective (and, hence, bijective, as domain and codomain have the same dimension) at every point in $\mathbb{M}(S)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm: Kernel projection equal to Lie derivatives} and \cite[Proposition 6.6]{ESrank2}, this is equivalent to proving that, for all $\gamma\in \mathrm M^*(S)$, the differential of $\mathrm{hol}\colon \mathrm M^*(S)\to \chi^{*}\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)$ at $\gamma$ has kernel given uniquely by elements of the form $\mathscr L_X\gamma$ for $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$. 

Consider $\dot \gamma\in T_{\gamma}\mathrm M^*(S)$ and assume that $\mathrm{d} \mathrm{hol}_{\gamma}(\dot\gamma)=0$. For simplicity, fix a path $\gamma_t\in \mathrm M^*(S)$ starting at $\gamma$ with tangent vector $\dot \gamma$. Let $\sigma_t\colon \widetilde S\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ be a smooth path of regular minimal immersions with immersion data $\gamma_t$ (constructed, for instance, using Proposition~\ref{prop: holo smooth dependence}). Denoting by $\rho_t\in \mathrm{Hom}\big(\pi_1(S), \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)$ the holonomy of $\sigma_t$, and recalling the description of the tangent space to the character variety from \ref{subsubsec:H^1}, the fact that $\mathrm{d} \mathrm{hol}_{\gamma}(\dot \gamma)=0$ implies that there exists $V\in \mathfrak g:=\mathrm{Lie}\big(\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)$ such that 
\[
\dot \rho \cdot {\rho}^{-1} = V- \mathrm{Ad}(\rho) (V)  \colon \pi_1(S)\to \mathfrak g~. 
\]
Hence, by replacing $\sigma_t$ with $\sigma'_t= \exp(-tV)\cdot  \sigma_t$, we get that $\sigma_t\in \mathscr U$ has holonomy $\rho_t'= \exp(-tV) \rho_t \exp(tV)$ and 
\[
\dot \rho' \cdot (\rho')^{-1}=  \mathrm{Ad}(\rho)(V)-V +\dot \rho =0~.
\]
Since, by assumption, $\sigma'_t$ is a path of minimal immersions and $\gamma$ is infinitesimally rigid, Proposition~\ref{prop: minimal deformations with trivial holonomy } implies that $\dot \sigma'=\mathrm{d}\sigma(\widetilde X)$ for some $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop: trivial sigma variation gives trivial gamma variation}, we conclude that $\dot\gamma=\mathscr L_X\gamma$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- defn-14: body_md -->
\label{def: complex hyperkahler}
A \emph{complex hyperKähler structure} on a complex manifold $\mathbb X$ with almost complex structure $\mathbf i$ is the data of a $\mathbf i$--holomorphic Riemannian metric $g$ on $\mathbb X$ (see Definition~\ref{def:holomorphic_riemannian_metric}) and of a triplet of tensors $\mathbb I, \mathbb J,\mathbb K\in \mathrm{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}(T^{1,0}\mathbb X)$ that satisfy the following properties:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\mathbb I, \mathbb J,\mathbb K$ are $\mathbf i$--holomorphic;
    \item $\mathbb I^2= \mathbb J^2=\mathbb K^2=\mathbb{IJK}=-\mathrm{Id}$;
    \item $g(\mathbb I\cdot, \mathbb I\cdot)= g(\mathbb J\cdot, \mathbb J\cdot)= g(\mathbb K\cdot, \mathbb K\cdot)= g(\cdot,\cdot)$;
    \item $D \mathbb I=D \mathbb J= D \mathbb K=0$, where $D$ is the holomorphic Levi-Civita connection of $g$.
\end{itemize}
\begin{remark}\label{rmk: hyperkahler symplectic forms}

We observe that, as in the case of hyperKähler structures, the pairing
$
\omega_{\mathbb L} :=  g(\mathbb L \cdot, \cdot)
$
defines three complex symplectic forms that are now holomorphic with respect to $\mathbf i$, as $\mathbb L$ varies in $\{\mathbb{I},\mathbb{J},\mathbb{K}\}$. 
\end{remark}
<!-- end defn-14 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rmk: hyperkahler symplectic forms}

We observe that, as in the case of hyperKähler structures, the pairing
$
\omega_{\mathbb L} :=  g(\mathbb L \cdot, \cdot)
$
defines three complex symplectic forms that are now holomorphic with respect to $\mathbf i$, as $\mathbb L$ varies in $\{\mathbb{I},\mathbb{J},\mathbb{K}\}$.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rmk:extending_tensors}
Using the splitting
\(
\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T\mathbb{X} = T^{1,0}\mathbb{X} \oplus T^{0,1}\mathbb{X} \cong T^{1,0}\mathbb{X} \oplus \overline{T^{1,0}\mathbb{X}},
\)
we can define a real tensor $g_{\mathbb{R}}$ on $T\mathbb{X}$ and endomorphisms $\mathbb{I}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{J}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{K}_{\mathbb{R}}$ on $T\mathbb{X}$ by setting
\begin{align*}
    &g_\mathbb R(\mathsf X,\mathsf Y):=2\Re\big(g(X,Y)\big),\quad \text{for} \ \mathsf X=X+\overline X\  \text{and} \ \mathsf Y=Y+\overline Y, \text{with} \ X,Y\in \Gamma(T^{1,0}\mathbb X) \\ & \mathbb L_\mathbb R(\mathsf X):=\mathbb{L}(X)+\overline{\mathbb{L}(X)},\quad \text{for} \ \mathsf X=X+\overline X\  \text{and} \ X\in\Gamma(T^{1,0}\mathbb X), 
\end{align*}
where $\mathbb L$ (resp. $\mathbb L_\mathbb R$) denotes one of the endomorphisms $\mathbb I,\mathbb J,\mathbb K$ (resp. $\mathbb I_\mathbb R,\mathbb J_\mathbb R,\mathbb K_\mathbb R$). As can be easily verified, the following properties hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The endomorphisms $\mathbb{I}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{J}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{K}_{\mathbb{R}}$ commute with $\mathbf{i}$ and they satisfy the quaternionic relations. Moreover, the $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$--linear extension of $\mathbb{L}_{\mathbb{R}}$ to $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T\mathbb{X}$ coincides with $\mathbb{L}$ when restricted over $T^{1,0}\mathbb{X}$, for every $\mathbb{L} \in \{\mathbb{I},\mathbb{J},\mathbb{K}\}$;
    \item $g_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a pseudo-Riemannian metric of neutral signature such that $g_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbf{i} \cdot, \mathbf{i} \cdot) = - g_{\mathbb{R}}$ and it is compatible with each of the three endomorphisms $\mathbb{I}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{J}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{K}_{\mathbb{R}}$ on $T\mathbb{X}$, meaning that $g_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{L}_{\mathbb{R}}\cdot,\mathbb{L}_{\mathbb{R}}\cdot) = g_{\mathbb{R}}$ for all $\mathbb{L} \in \{\mathbb{I},\mathbb{J},\mathbb{K}\}$; observe that the $\mathbb{C}$-bilinear extension of $g_{\mathbb R}$ to $\mathbb C T\mathbb X$ restricts to $g$ on $T^{1,0}\mathbb X$ and to zero on $T^{0,1}\mathbb X$.
    \item the non-degenerate $2$--forms $\omega_{\mathbb{L}}^{\mathbb R}:=g_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb{L}_{\mathbb R}\cdot, \cdot)$, for $\mathbb{L}_{\mathbb R} \in \{\mathbb{I}_{\mathbb R},\mathbb{J}_{\mathbb R},\mathbb{K}_{\mathbb R}\}$, are closed and, hence, determine three real symplectic forms;
    
\end{enumerate}

Although not strictly necessary for this paper, we find worthwile to explain that the almost-complex structures $\mathbb{I}_{\mathbb R}, \mathbb{J}_{\mathbb{R}}$ and $\mathbb{K}_{\mathbb{R}}$ are integrable in the classical (complex) sense.

\begin{lem}\label{lemma integrable almost complex for complex hyper}
    Given a complex hyperKähler structure on a complex manifold $(\mathbb X,\mathbf i)$, the endomorphisms $\mathbb{I}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{J}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{K}_{\mathbb{R}}$ are integrable almost-complex structures.
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
    We shall show that the Nijenhuis $N_{\mathbb L_{\mathbb R}}$ vanishes identically, for $\mathbb L=\mathbb I,\mathbb J,\mathbb K$. 

For this purpose, just as for almost complex structures defined on the real tangent bundle, let us introduce a Nijenhuis tensor associated with the endomorphism \(\mathbb L\) as follows:
$$N_{\mathbb L}(X,Y):=[X,Y]+\mathbb L\big([\mathbb LX,Y]+[X,\mathbb LY]\big)-[\mathbb LX,\mathbb LY]\in T^{1,0}\mathbb X, \quad \text{for} \ X,Y\in T^{1,0}\mathbb X.$$
Indeed, since the almost complex structure \(\mathbf{i}\) is integrable, the distribution \(T^{1,0}\mathbb X\) is involutive, and therefore \(N_{\mathbb L}\) defines a well-defined \((1,2)\)-tensor on the holomorphic tangent bundle.  As in the classical setting, this condition  follows from the fact that the endomorphisms \(\mathbb L\) are parallel with respect to the holomorphic Levi--Civita connection (Definition~\ref{def: complex hyperkahler}).

Now, as a consequence of the identity 
\begin{equation}\label{eq: Nijen real and complex}
    N_{\mathbb L_{\mathbb R}}(\mathsf X,\mathsf Y)=2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(N_{\mathbb L}(X,Y)\bigr)
\end{equation}
where \(\mathsf X=X+\overline{X}\) and \(\mathsf Y=Y+\overline{Y}\), we deduce that $N_{\mathbb L_{\mathbb R}}=0$. The relation~\eqref{eq: Nijen real and complex} between the Nijenhuis tensors follows directly from the definition of \(\mathbb L_{\mathbb R}\) and from the fact that \([\overline{X},Y]=0\) for \(X,Y\in T^{1,0}\mathbb X\), after choosing local holomorphic extensions.
\end{proof}

In summary, from Remark~\ref{rmk:extending_tensors} and Lemma~\ref{lemma integrable almost complex for complex hyper} the quadruple $(g_{\mathbb R}, \mathbb{I}_{\mathbb R}, \mathbb{J}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{K}_{\mathbb{R}})$ has the same algebraic and differential geometric properties as a classical hyperK\"ahler structure on $\mathbb{X}$, except for the fact that $g_{\mathbb R}$ is indefinite (compare with \cite{Bridgeland2021}).
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{lemma integrable almost complex for complex hyper}
    Given a complex hyperKähler structure on a complex manifold $(\mathbb X,\mathbf i)$, the endomorphisms $\mathbb{I}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{J}_{\mathbb{R}}, \mathbb{K}_{\mathbb{R}}$ are integrable almost-complex structures.
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
We shall show that the Nijenhuis $N_{\mathbb L_{\mathbb R}}$ vanishes identically, for $\mathbb L=\mathbb I,\mathbb J,\mathbb K$. 

For this purpose, just as for almost complex structures defined on the real tangent bundle, let us introduce a Nijenhuis tensor associated with the endomorphism \(\mathbb L\) as follows:
$$N_{\mathbb L}(X,Y):=[X,Y]+\mathbb L\big([\mathbb LX,Y]+[X,\mathbb LY]\big)-[\mathbb LX,\mathbb LY]\in T^{1,0}\mathbb X, \quad \text{for} \ X,Y\in T^{1,0}\mathbb X.$$
Indeed, since the almost complex structure \(\mathbf{i}\) is integrable, the distribution \(T^{1,0}\mathbb X\) is involutive, and therefore \(N_{\mathbb L}\) defines a well-defined \((1,2)\)-tensor on the holomorphic tangent bundle.  As in the classical setting, this condition  follows from the fact that the endomorphisms \(\mathbb L\) are parallel with respect to the holomorphic Levi--Civita connection (Definition~\ref{def: complex hyperkahler}).

Now, as a consequence of the identity 
\begin{equation}\label{eq: Nijen real and complex}
    N_{\mathbb L_{\mathbb R}}(\mathsf X,\mathsf Y)=2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(N_{\mathbb L}(X,Y)\bigr)
\end{equation}
where \(\mathsf X=X+\overline{X}\) and \(\mathsf Y=Y+\overline{Y}\), we deduce that $N_{\mathbb L_{\mathbb R}}=0$. The relation~\eqref{eq: Nijen real and complex} between the Nijenhuis tensors follows directly from the definition of \(\mathbb L_{\mathbb R}\) and from the fact that \([\overline{X},Y]=0\) for \(X,Y\in T^{1,0}\mathbb X\), after choosing local holomorphic extensions.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:integrability_complex_hyperkahler}
Let $\mathbb X$ be a complex manifold and let $\mathbf i$ be the associated integrable almost-complex structure on $T\mathbb X$. Suppose that there exist three $\mathbf{i}$--holomorphic sections $\mathbb{I},\mathbb{J},\mathbb{K}$ of $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{C}}(T^{1,0}\mathbb X)$ such that $\mathbb I^2= \mathbb J^2=\mathbb K^2=\mathbb{I}\mathbb{J}\mathbb{K}=-\mathrm{Id}$ and an $\mathbf i$--holomorphic Riemannian metric $g$ compatible with $\mathbb{I}$, $\mathbb{J}$, and $\mathbb{K}$. 

If the 2-forms $\omega_\mathbb L=g(\mathbb L\cdot,\cdot)$ are closed for each $\mathbb L\in\{\mathbb{I},\mathbb{J},\mathbb{K}\}$, then the quadruple $(\mathbb{I},\mathbb{J},\mathbb{K},g)$ defines a complex hyperK\"ahler structure on $\mathbb X$.
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
We first observe that it is enough to prove that \(N_{\mathbb L}\equiv 0\) for every \(\mathbb L\in\{\mathbb I,\mathbb J,\mathbb K\}\). Indeed, once this is established, the classical formula in \cite[Chapter IX, Proposition 4.2]{kobayashi1996foundations}, extended to the present holomorphic setting, implies directly that if the symplectic forms \(\omega_{\mathbb L}\) are closed, then \(D\mathbb L=0\). In the classical setting of almost complex structures defined on the smooth tangent bundle of a manifold, the vanishing of the Nijenhuis tensor is equivalent to the involutivity of the holomorphic, or equivalently anti-holomorphic, tangent distribution. In our setting, as we shall explain shortly, in order to prove that \(N_{\mathbb L}\equiv 0\), we need to show that both eigendistributions \(\operatorname{Eig}_{\pm i}(\mathbb L)\) are involutive. Indeed, imposing the involutivity conditions
\[
\mathbb L\bigl([X\mp i\,\mathbb L(X),Y\mp i\,\mathbb L(Y)]\bigr)=\pm i\,[X\mp i\,\mathbb L(X),Y\mp i\,\mathbb L(Y)]
\]
and expanding the brackets, one finds that the holomorphic vector field \(N_{\mathbb L}(X,Y)\) belongs to both \(\operatorname{Eig}_i(\mathbb L)\) and  \(\operatorname{Eig}_{-i}(\mathbb L)\). Since these two eigenspaces have trivial intersection, this is possible if and only if \(N_{\mathbb L}(X,Y)=0\).
