                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
In the following, we will only show that $\operatorname{Eig}_i(\mathbb K)\subset T^{1,0}\mathbb X$ is involutive, since the computations for the \((-i)\)-eigenspace and the other endomorphisms are analogous. Given $Y,Z\in\Gamma(T^{1,0}\mathbb X)$, we have $$
\omega_{\mathbb I}(Y,Z)=g(\mathbb I(Y),Z)=-g(\mathbb{K}(Y),\mathbb{J}(Z))=-\omega_{\mathbb J}(Z,\mathbb{K}(Y))=\omega_{\mathbb J}(\mathbb{K}(Y),Z),
$$
hence $\iota_{Y}\omega_{\mathbb{I}}=\iota_{\mathbb{K}(Y)}\omega_{\mathbb{J}}$. In particular, $\mathbb{K}(Y)=i \, Y$ if and only if $\iota_Y\omega_{\mathbb{I}}=i\, \iota_{Y}\omega_{\mathbb{J}}$. In what follows, we denote by $\mathscr L$ the complex Lie derivative introduced in Section~\ref{subsec: complex lie derivatives}, which acts naturally on any space of tensors defined on $\mathbb X$ with complex values, and differentiates them along a complex vector field in $\mathbb{C}T \mathbb X$. Suppose that $\mathbb{K}(Y)=i\, Y$ and $\mathbb{K}(Z)=i\, Z$, then \begin{align*}
    \iota_{[Y,Z]}\omega_{\mathbb{I}}&=\mathscr{L}_Y\big(\iota_{Z}\omega_\mathbb{I}\big)-\iota_Z\big(\mathscr{L}_Y\omega_\mathbb{I}\big) \\ &=\mathscr{L}_Y\big(i\,\iota_{Z}\omega_\mathbb{J}\big)-\iota_Z\big(\mathscr{L}_Y\omega_\mathbb{I}\big) \\ &=\mathscr{L}_Y\big(i\,\iota_{Z}\omega_\mathbb{J}\big)-\iota_Z\mathrm d(\iota_Y\omega_\mathbb{I}) \tag{Cartan's magic formula and $\omega_\mathbb{I}$ closed}\\ &=\mathscr{L}_Y\big(i\,\iota_{Z}\omega_\mathbb{J}\big)-\iota_Z\mathrm d\big(i\,\iota_Y\omega_\mathbb{J}\big) \\ &=\mathscr{L}_Y\big(i\,\iota_{Z}\omega_\mathbb{J}\big)-i\,\iota_Z\mathscr{L}_Y\omega_\mathbb{J} \tag{Cartan's magic formula and $\omega_\mathbb{J}$ closed} \\ &=i\,\iota_{[Y,Z]}\omega_\mathbb{J},
\end{align*} and this is equivalent to $\mathbb{K}\big([Y,Z]\big)=i\,[Y,Z].$
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- defn-15: body_md -->
\label{def: hyperkahler}
    A \emph{hyperKähler structure} on a smooth manifold $\mathbb{Y}$ is the datum of a 4-tuple $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{I},\mathbf{J},\mathbf{K})$, where $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{I})$, $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{J})$ and $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{K})$ are all Kähler structures, and  $\mathbf{I},\mathbf{J},\mathbf{K}$ satisfy the quaternionic identities $\mathbf{I}^2=\mathbf{J}^2=\mathbf{K}^2=\mathbf{I}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{K}=-\mathrm{Id}$.
<!-- end defn-15 -->
<!-- thm-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:hyperkahler_almost_fuchsian}
Let $S$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $\ge 2$, then the almost-Fuchsian space $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ admits a $\mathrm{MCG}(S)$--invariant hyperK\"ahler structure $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{I},\mathbf{J},\mathbf{K})$. Moreover, the Fuchsian locus $\mathcal{F}(S)$ is an $\mathbf{I}$--holomorphic, totally geodesic submanifold and $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{I})$ restricts to a multiple of the Weil-Petersson K\"ahler metric on Teichm\"uller space.
<!-- end thm-12 -->
<!-- prop-14: body_md -->
\label{prop: lemma I trautwein}The complex structure $\mathbf{I}$ in Donaldson's hyperKähler metric is obtained as the pull-back via $\pi_{\mathcal AF}$ of the complex structure on $\mathbb{QD}(S)$ acting as the multiplication by $i$ on elements $[\dot \mu,\dot q]$.
<!-- end prop-14 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
\label{prop: omega J pullback AF}
Let $\Omega^{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}:=-\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}$ be the standard complex symplectic form on $T^*\mathcal T(S)\cong\mathbb{QD}(S)$ obtained from the complex Liouville $1$--form. Then, the complex structure $\mathbf{J}$ in Donaldson's hyperKähler metric satisfies:
 $$\omega_{\mathbf J}=2\pi_{\mathcal{AF}}^*\Im(\Omega^{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}).$$
<!-- end prop-15 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem: convention on I}
In the original paper by Donaldson \cite{donaldson2003} and subsequently in \cite{trautwein2018infinite}, the complex structure $\mathbf{I}$ when restricted to the Fuchsian locus, differs by a sign from the one introduced in Section~\ref{sec: beltrami differentials}, since it is compatible with the opposite orientation on Teichmüller space (see Proposition~\ref{prop: lemma I trautwein}). In fact, our convention is consistent with the one used by Hodge \cite{hodge2005hyperkahler}. To avoid sign propagation and to simplify notation, in this article we will denote by $\mathbf{I}$ the complex structure which, when restricted to $\mathcal{T}(S)$, coincides exactly with the one defined in Section~\ref{sec: beltrami differentials}
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- prop-16: body_md -->
\label{prop: Hodge structure J and omega G}
The following identities hold for Donaldson's hyperKähler structure $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{I},\mathbf{J},\mathbf{K})$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] $(\mathrm{hol}_{\mathcal{AF}})^* J_\chi=-\mathbf J$;
    \item[(ii)] $2(\mathrm{hol}_{\mathcal{AF}})^*\omega_G=\omega_{\mathbf I}+i\,\omega_{\mathbf K}$,
\end{itemize}where $\omega_G$ is the Goldman's symplectic form on $\chi^{irr}\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})\big)$ and $\omega_{\mathbf L}=\mathbf g(\mathbf L\cdot,\cdot)$ for $\mathbf L\in\{\mathbf I,\mathbf J,\mathbf K\}$.
<!-- end prop-16 -->
<!-- defn-16: body_md -->
\label{def:para-complex structure}
    A \emph{para-complex structure} on a smooth manifold $\mathbb{Y}$ is the datum of a section $\mathbf{P} \in \Gamma(\mathrm{End}(T \mathbb{Y}))$ that satisfies the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\mathbf{P}^2 = \mathrm{Id}$;
        \item the $(+1)$--eigenspace $V_y^+$ and the $(-1)$--eigenspace $V_y^-$ of $\mathbf{P}_y$ inside $T_y \mathbb{Y}$ have the same dimension for any $y \in \mathbb{Y}$;
        \item the distributions $\{V_y^+\}_{y \in \mathbb{Y}}$ and $\{V_y^-\}_{y \in \mathbb{Y}}$ are involutive. 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end defn-16 -->
<!-- defn-17: body_md -->
A \emph{para-Kähler structure} is the datum of a pair $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf P)$ where $\mathbf{g}$ is a pseudo-Riemannian metric of neutral signature, $\mathbf P$ is a para-complex structure, and $\mathbf{g}(\mathbf P\cdot,\cdot)$ is a symplectic form.
<!-- end defn-17 -->
<!-- defn-18: body_md -->
\label{def: para-hyperkahler}
    A \emph{para-hyperKähler structure} on a smooth manifold $\mathbb{Y}$ is the datum of a 4-tuple $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{I},\mathbf{J},\mathbf{K})$, where $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{I})$ is a Kähler structure, while $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{J})$ and $(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{K})$ are para-Kähler structures, and  $\mathbf{I},\mathbf{J},\mathbf{K}$ satisfy the para-quaternionic identities $\mathbf{I}^2=-\mathrm{Id}$, $\mathbf{J}^2=\mathbf{K}^2=\mathbf{I}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{K}=\mathrm{Id}$.
<!-- end defn-18 -->
<!-- thm-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:para_hyperkahler}
Let $S$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $\ge 2$, then $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ admits a $\mathrm{MCG}(S)$--invariant para-hyperK\"ahler structure $(\mathbf{g}',\mathbf{I}',\mathbf{J}',\mathbf{K}')$. Moreover, the Fuchsian locus $\mathcal{F}(S)$ is an $\mathbf{I}'$--holomorphic, totally geodesic submanifold and $(\mathbf{g}',\mathbf{I}')$ restricts to twice the Weil-Petersson K\"ahler metric on Teichm\"uller space.
<!-- end thm-13 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rmk: convention I'}
The same situation as in Remark~\ref{rem: convention on I} also applies in this case, due to the convention adopted in \cite{MazSepTamb}, that is, the complex structure $\mathbf{I}'$ used in this exposition is equal to the opposite of the complex structure considered in \cite{MazSepTamb}.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- prop-17: body_md -->
The complex structure $\mathbf{I}$ compatible with the para-hyperKähler metric on $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ is obtained as the pull-back via $\pi_{\mathcal{MGH}}$ of the complex structure on $\mathbb{QD}(S)$ acting as the multiplication by $i$ on elements $[\dot \mu,\dot q]$.
<!-- end prop-17 -->
<!-- prop-18: body_md -->
\label{prop: omega J' and Omega MST}
Let $\Omega^{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}=-\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}$ be the standard complex symplectic form on $T^*\mathcal T(S)\cong\mathbb{QD}(S)$ obtained from the complex Liouville $1$--form. Then, the complex structure $\mathbf{J'}$ compatible with the para-hyperKähler metric on $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ satisfies:
 $$\omega_{\mathbf J'}=2\pi_{\mathcal{MGH}}^*\Re(\Omega^{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}})$$
<!-- end prop-18 -->
<!-- thm-14: body_md -->
\label{thm: Thm C and Cor H}
The following identities hold for the para-hyperKähler metric $(\mathbf{g}',\mathbf{I}',\mathbf{J}',\mathbf{K}')$ on $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] $(\mathrm{hol}_{\mathcal{MGH}})^*(\mathrm{Id},-\mathrm{Id})=\mathbf J'$;\vspace{0.5em}
    \item[(ii)] $\displaystyle(\mathrm{hol}_{\mathcal{MGH}})^*\big(\pi_l^*\omega_{G}^\mathbb R+\pi_r^*\omega_G^\mathbb R\big)=\,\omega_{\mathbf I'}$. 
\end{itemize}
where $\omega_G^\mathbb R$ denotes the Goldman symplectic form on $\chi^{irr}\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)\big)$ and
\[
\pi_l, \pi_r : \chi^*\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)^2\big) \to \chi^{irr}\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)\big)
\]
denote the projections onto the first and second component of the representations.
<!-- end thm-14 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{lem: I_0 is holomorphic}
The tensor $\mathbb{I}_0$ is holomorphic with respect to the natural complex structure of $\mathbb{QD}(S) \times \mathbb{QD}(\overline{S})$ described above.
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Set $\mathbb{U}:=\mathbb{QD}(S)\times \mathbb{QD}(\overline S)$. We show that \(\mathbb I_0\) is a holomorphic section of \(\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}(T^{1,0}\mathbb U)\). Since holomorphicity is a local property, let \((z_1,\dots,z_n,w_1,\dots,w_n)\) be local holomorphic coordinates on \(\mathbb U\), where \((z_1,\dots,z_n)\) are holomorphic coordinates on \(\mathbb{QD}(S)\), and \((w_1,\dots,w_n)\) are holomorphic coordinates on \(\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)\). Then $ \frac{\partial}{\partial z_1},\dots,\frac{\partial}{\partial z_n},
\frac{\partial}{\partial w_1},\dots,\frac{\partial}{\partial w_n}$
is a local holomorphic frame of \(T^{1,0}\mathbb{U}\). By definition of \(\mathbb I_0\), one has
$$ \mathbb I_0\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial z_j}\right)=i\frac{\partial}{\partial z_j}, \qquad \mathbb I_0\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial w_k}\right)=-i\frac{\partial}{\partial w_k}.$$
Therefore, with respect to the above holomorphic frame, the matrix of \(\mathbb I_0\) is $$\begin{pmatrix}i\,\mathrm{Id}_{n} & 0\\ 0 &  -i\,\mathrm{Id}_{n} \end{pmatrix}.$$
Its coefficients are constant, hence holomorphic. Thus \(\mathbb I_0\) is a holomorphic section of $\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}\big(T^{1,0}\mathbb U\big)$, as claimed.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rmk: identification of real tangent bundle}
By Proposition~\ref{prop: AF and MGH are totally real submanifolds}, both $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ are totally real submanifolds of $\mathbb M_0(S)$ (with respect to $\mathbf{i}$). There is a natural identification of $T\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $T\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ as totally real subbundles of $T^{1,0}\mathbb{M}_{0}(S)$ defined by sending a tangent vector $v$ to $\frac{1}{2}(v-i\,\mathbf{i}(v))$. From now on, we will tacitly use these embeddings so that we can consider the action of $\mathbb{I}$ on $T \mathcal{AF}(S)$ and on $T\mathcal{MGH}(S)$. We observe that this is equivalent to considering the restriction of $\mathbb{I}_{\mathbb{R}}$ to the real tangent bundles to the submanifolds (see Remark~\ref{rmk:extending_tensors}). We will use this same strategy for the other tensors $\mathbb{J}$ and $\mathbb{K}$ that will be part of the complex hyperK\"ahler structure and will be defined later in this section.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- prop-19: body_md -->
\label{prop: restriction of I}
    The operator $\mathbb I$ restricts to $\mathbf{I}$ on $T \mathcal{AF}(S)$ and to $\mathbf{I}'$ on $T\mathcal{MGH}(S)$.
<!-- end prop-19 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
We will carry out the proof for the tensor $\mathbf{I}$, since the argument for $\mathbf{I}'$ is analogous. The complex structure $\mathbf{I}$ is equal to the pull-back, via the map $\pi_{\mathcal{AF}}$ from Section~\ref{sec: hyperKahler almost-fuchsian}, of the endomorphism $[\dot\mu, \dot q]\mapsto [i\dot\mu, i\dot q]$ on the real tangent bundle $T\mathbb{QD}(S)$ (see Proposition~\ref{prop: lemma I trautwein} and Remark~\ref{rem: convention on I}). In accordance with the description of the almost-Fuchsian locus in~\eqref{eq:inclusion AF in M}, any $v \in T\mathcal{AF}(S)\subset T^{1,0}\mathbb M_0(S)$ can be written as $v=[\dot\mu,\dot q,\dot{\overline \mu},\dot{\overline q},\dot u]$. Since $\mathbb{I}$ was constructed as the pull-back of the complex structure $\mathbb{I}_0$ defined in~\eqref{eq: def I in trivialization of pi}, it follows that applying $\mathbb{I}$ to a vector $v \in T\mathcal{AF}(S)$ described as above yields exactly the action of $\mathbf{I}$ on the model $T\mathcal{AF}(S)$ inside $T^{1,0}\mathbb M_0(S)$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{lem: J_0 holomorphic}
The tensor $\mathbb{J}_0$ is holomorphic with respect to the natural complex structure \((J_\chi,J_\chi)\) of $\chi^*\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big)$ described above.
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- prop-20: body_md -->
\label{prop: restriction of J}
    The tensor $\mathbb J$ restricts to $\mathbf{J}$ on $\mathcal{AF}(S)$, and the tensor $\mathbf i\circ\mathbb J$ restricts to $\mathbf{J}'$ on $\mathcal {MGH}(S)$.
<!-- end prop-20 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Regarding the restriction to the almost-Fuchsian locus, it suffices to work at the level of smooth character varieties by diagram~\eqref{eq:comm diag AF}. In fact, 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
by Proposition~\ref{prop: Hodge structure J and omega G} point $(i)$ it is enough to prove that the action of the endomorphism $\mathbb J_0$ on the subspace $(\Delta^\dagger)_*\big(H^1(S,\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C})_{\mathrm{Ad}\rho})\big)$ is equal to the multiplication by $-i$.
This is a direct computation by using Equation $\eqref{eq: definition J_0}$\begin{align*}
        \mathbb J_0(\sigma\otimes\phi,-\sigma\otimes\overline{{}^t\phi})&=\big(-J_\chi(\sigma\otimes\phi),J_\chi(-\sigma\otimes\overline{{}^t\phi})\big) \\ &=(-\sigma\otimes i\phi,-\sigma\otimes i\, \overline{{}^t\phi}) .
    \end{align*}
    The last term in the equation belongs to the image of \(H^1(S,\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C})_{\mathrm{Ad}\rho})\) via $\mathrm{d}\Delta^\dagger$; indeed, 
    \[
    -\overline{{}^t(-\sigma\otimes i\phi)} = - (-\sigma) \otimes (- i \, \overline{{}^t\phi}) = -\sigma\otimes i\, \overline{{}^t\phi} .
    \]
     On the other hand, regarding the restriction to \(\mathcal{MGH}(S)\), we observe that
     \[\mathbf i\circ\mathbb J=\mathrm{hol}^*(J_\chi,J_\chi)\circ\mathrm{hol}^*\mathbb J_0=\mathrm{hol}^*\big((J_\chi,J_\chi)\circ\mathbb J_0\big)=\mathrm{hol}^*(\mathrm{Id,-\mathrm{Id}}).\] Last chains of equalities directly implies the claim by diagram~\eqref{eq:comm diag MGH} and Theorem~\ref{thm: Thm C and Cor H}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- prop-21: body_md -->
\label{prop: restriction of K}
   The tensor $\mathbb K$ satisfies $\mathbb K^2=-\mathrm{Id}$. Moreover, $\mathbb{K}$ restricts to $\mathbf K$ on $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathbf i\circ\mathbb K$ restricts to $\mathbf K'$ on $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$.
<!-- end prop-21 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Since $\mathbf{IJ}=\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf I'\mathbf{J'}=\mathbf K'$, we easily get that $\mathbb K$ restricts to $\mathbf K$ on $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathbf i\circ\mathbb K$ restricts to $\mathbf K'$ on $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$. Now, the tensors $\mathbb K^2$ and $-\mathrm{Id}$ are $\mathbf i$--holomorphic endomorphisms of $T^{1,0}\mathbb M_0(S)$ and they coincide on $\mathcal{AF}(S)$, which is a totally real submanifold of $\mathbb M_0(S)$ of full dimension. By Lemma~\ref{lem: fundamental lem analytic continuation} and Remark~\ref{rmk: fundamental_lemma_applied to tensors}, we conclude that $\mathbb K^2=-\mathrm{Id}$ everywhere on $\mathbb{M}_0(S)$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{lem: compatibility_omega_I}
The complex symplectic form $\omega_\mathbb I$ restricts to $\omega_\mathbf I$ on the almost-Fuchsian locus $\mathcal{AF}(S)$. As a consequence,
\[
    \omega_{\mathbb I} (\mathbb I\cdot, \cdot)+\omega_{\mathbb I} (\cdot,\mathbb I\cdot)=0.
    \]
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The tensors $\omega_\mathbb I$ and $\mathbb I$ are both $\mathbf i$--holomorphic and $\mathbb I$ restricts to $\mathbf I$ on $T\mathcal{AF}(S)\subset T^{1,0}\mathbb M_0(S)$ (see Proposition~\ref{prop: restriction of I}). If we show that $\omega_{\mathbb{I}}\vert_{\mathcal{AF}(S)} = \omega_{\mathbf{I}}$, then we can conclude the proof by Lemma~\ref{lem: fundamental lem analytic continuation}, since $\omega_{\mathbf{I}}$ is compatible with $\mathbf{I}$ on $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:hyperkahler_almost_fuchsian}. In fact, it suffices to prove that
\[
\omega_{\mathbb{I}}\vert_{\mathcal{AF}(S)} =2(\mathrm{hol}_{\mathcal{AF}})^*\Re(\omega_G),
\]
which in turn coincides with $\omega_{\mathbf{I}}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop: Hodge structure J and omega G} point $(ii)$. The differential of the map $$\Delta^\dagger : \chi^{irr}\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})\big) \to \chi^*\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2\big),$$  is given by $\dot\rho\mapsto (\dot\rho,-\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}'})$. Therefore, to understand the restriction \(\omega_{\mathbb{I}}|_{\mathcal{AF}(S)}\), according to diagram~\eqref{eq:comm diag AF}, we need to compute the element
\begin{equation}\label{eq: formula in Lemma for Goldman}
 (\pi_r^* \omega_G)\big((\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_2),(\dot\rho_1',\dot\rho_2')\big)+(\pi_l^*\omega_G)\big((\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_2),(\dot\rho_1',\dot\rho_2')\big)
\end{equation}
under the conditions \(\dot{\rho}_2 = -{\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}_1}}\) and \(\dot{\rho}_2' = -{\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}_1'}}\). Hence, by using the description of Goldman's symplectic form from Equation~\eqref{eq: Goldman symplectic form explicit formula}, the term in~\eqref{eq: formula in Lemma for Goldman} is equal to
\begin{align*}
    \omega_G\big(-{\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}_1}},-{\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}_1'}}\big)+\omega_G(\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_1')& =  \sum_{h,k} \int_S\Big(\mathrm{tr}(\overline{{}^t\phi_{1,h}} \cdot \overline{{}^t\phi_{1,k}'})+\mathrm{tr}(\phi_{1,h} \cdot \phi_{1,k}')\Big)\, \sigma_{1,h}\wedge\sigma_{1,k}' \\
  &=2\sum_{h,k} \int_S\Re\big(\mathrm{tr}(\phi_{1,h} \cdot \phi_{1,k}')\big)\, \sigma_{1,h}\wedge\sigma_{1,k}' \\
  &=2\Re(\omega_G)(\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_1'),
\end{align*}
where we selected representatives $\sum_h \sigma_{1,h}\otimes \phi_{1,h}$ and $\sum_k \sigma_{1,k}'\otimes \phi_{1,k}'$ of $\dot{\rho}_1$ and $\dot{\rho}_1'$, respectively. This concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- prop-22: body_md -->
\label{prop: formula for omega_K}
    The complex symplectic form $\omega_{\mathbb K}$ satisfies:
    \[ \omega_{\mathbb K} =i\mathrm{hol}^*\left( \pi_r^* \omega_G- \pi_l^*\omega_G\right).\] In particular, $\omega_\mathbb K$ is a closed $2$--form.
<!-- end prop-22 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
We begin by observing that $\omega_\mathbb{K}=\omega_\mathbb{I}(\mathbb{J}\cdot,\cdot)$, as the following computation shows:
$$
\omega_\mathbb{K}
= g(\mathbb{K}\cdot,\cdot)
= \omega_\mathbb{I}(\mathbb{K}\cdot,\mathbb{I}\cdot)
= -\omega_\mathbb{I}(\mathbb{I}\mathbb{K}\cdot,\cdot)
= \omega_\mathbb{I}(\mathbb{J}\cdot,\cdot).
$$ In particular, by Proposition~\ref{prop: restriction of J} and Lemma~\ref{lem: compatibility_omega_I}, this implies $\omega_{\mathbb K}|_{\mathcal{AF}(S)}=\omega_{\mathbf I}(\mathbf J\cdot,\cdot)=\omega_\mathbf K=2(\mathrm{hol}_{\mathcal{AF}})^*\big(\Im\omega_G\big)$ (see Proposition~\ref{prop: Hodge structure J and omega G} point $(ii)$).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
At this point, it is sufficient to prove the equality between                                                                                                             
$i\big(\pi_r^* \omega_G- \pi_l^*\omega_G\big)$ and $2\Im\omega_G$ on the image of the $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$--character variety via the map $\Delta^\dagger$ (see diagram~\eqref{eq:comm diag AF}). Indeed, once the equality is established on the almost-Fuchsian locus, the claim follows by applying Lemma~\ref{lem: fundamental lem analytic continuation}. The computation is similar to the one performed in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem: compatibility_omega_I}, namely
\begin{align*}
i(\pi_r^* \omega_G)\big((\dot\rho_1,-\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}_1}),(\dot\rho_1',-\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}_1'})\big)&-i(\pi_l^*\omega_G)\big((\dot\rho_1,-\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}_1}),(\dot\rho_1',-\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}_1'})\big)= \\
&=i\Big(\omega_G\big(\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}_1},\overline{{}^t\dot{\rho}_1'}\big)-\omega_G(\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_1')\Big) \\
&=i \sum_{h,k} \int_S \Big(\overline{\mathrm{tr}(\phi_{1,h} \cdot \phi_{1,k}')}-\mathrm{tr}(\phi_{1,h} \cdot \phi_{1,k}')\Big)\,\sigma_{1,h}\wedge\sigma'_{1,k} \\ 
&=-2i^2(\Im\omega_G)(\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_1') \\ &=2(\Im\omega_G)(\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_1').
\end{align*}
where we selected representatives $\sum_h \sigma_{1,h}\otimes \phi_{1,h}$ and $\sum_k \sigma_{1,k}'\otimes \phi_{1,k}'$ of $\dot{\rho}_1$ and $\dot{\rho}_1'$, respectively.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- prop-23: body_md -->
The $2$--form $\omega_\mathbb J$ is compatible with $\mathbb J$, namely
    $$\omega_\mathbb J(\mathbb J\cdot,\cdot)+\omega_\mathbb J(\cdot,\mathbb J\cdot)=0.$$
<!-- end prop-23 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
From Proposition $\ref{prop: restriction of I}$ and Lemma $\ref{lem: compatibility_omega_I}$ we know that the holomorphic metric $g=\omega_{\mathbb I}(\cdot,\mathbb I\cdot)$ restricts to the Riemannian metric $\mathbf g$ on $\mathcal{AF}(S)$. Moreover, by Proposition $\ref{prop: restriction of J}$ we have $\mathbb J|_{\mathcal{AF}(S)}=\mathbf J$. We can therefore deduce that \begin{align*}
\omega_{\mathbb J}(\mathbb J\cdot,\cdot)|_{\mathcal{AF}(S)}&=g(\mathbb J^2\cdot,\cdot)|_{\mathcal{AF}(S)} \\ &=-\mathbf g \\ &=-\mathbf{g}(\mathbf J\cdot,\mathbf J\cdot) \tag{$\mathbf g$ is compatible with $\mathbf J$} \\ &=-g(\mathbb J\cdot,\mathbb J\cdot)|_{\mathcal{AF}(S)} \\&=-\omega_{\mathbb J}(\cdot,\mathbb J\cdot)|_{\mathcal{AF}(S)}
\end{align*}and we conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem: fundamental lem analytic continuation}.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- prop-24: body_md -->
The complex symplectic form $\omega_{\mathbb J}$ satisfies:
    \[
    \omega_{\mathbb J}=-\pi^*\Omega(\mathbb{I}\cdot, \cdot).
    \]
    In particular, $\omega_\mathbb J$ is a closed $2$--form.
<!-- end prop-24 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Let
\(\dot{\gamma},\dot{\gamma}'\)
be tangent vectors to $\mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\bar S)$ in the image of $\mathrm{d}\pi|_{T\mathcal{AF}(S)}$. Then \begin{align*}
\Omega(\mathbb{I}\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma')&=\Omega([i\dot\mu,-i\overline{\dot\mu},i\dot q,-i\overline{\dot q}],[\dot\mu',\overline{\dot\mu'},\dot q',\overline{\dot q'}]) \\ &=\Omega^{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}([i\dot\mu,i\dot q],[\dot\mu',\dot q'])+\overline{\Omega^{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}([i\dot\mu,i\dot q],[\dot\mu',\dot q'])} \\ &=-2\operatorname{Im}\big(\Omega^{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}([\dot\mu,\dot q],[\dot\mu',\dot q'])\big).
\end{align*}
By the discussion preceding the statement, \(\pi^*\Omega\) is an \(\mathbf{i}\)-holomorphic symplectic form on \(\mathbb{M}_0(S)\), and therefore Lemma~\ref{lem: fundamental lem analytic continuation}, together with the identity \(2\pi_{\mathcal{AF}}^*\mathrm{Im}(\Omega^{\mathbb{C}})|_{\mathcal{AF}(S)}=\omega_{\mathbf{J}}\) from Proposition~\ref{prop: omega J pullback AF}, implies that
\(\omega_{\mathbb{J}}=-\pi^*\Omega(\mathbb{I}\cdot, \cdot)\) (see also Remark~\ref{rmk: restriction of pi on AF and MGH}).
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
The $\mathbf i$--holomorphic complex structures $\mathbb I,\mathbb J,\mathbb K$ together with the $\mathbf i$--holomorphic metric $g$ defines a $\mathrm{MCG}(S)$--invariant complex hyperK\"ahler structure on $\mathbb M_0(S)$.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{cor: restriction of complex hyperkahler to AF e MSH}
The complex hyperK\"ahler structure on $\mathbb M_0(S)$ satisfies the following conditions: \begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] the quadruple $(\mathbb I,\mathbb{J},\mathbb{K},g)$ restricts to Donaldson's hyperk\"ahler metric $(\mathbf I,\mathbf J,\mathbf K,\mathbf g)$ on the almost-Fuchsian locus $\mathcal{AF}(S)$;
    \item[(ii)] the quadruple $(\mathbb I,\mathbf i\circ\mathbb{J},\mathbf i\circ\mathbb{K},g)$ restricts to the para-hyperK\"ahler metric $(\mathbf{I}',\mathbf{J}',\mathbf{K}',\mathbf g')$ of Mazzoli-Seppi-Tamburelli on the Anti-de Sitter locus $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Thanks to Propositions~\ref{prop: restriction of I},~\ref{prop: restriction of J} and~\ref{prop: restriction of K}, we already know that the three complex structures $\mathbb{I}, \mathbb{J}, \mathbb{K}$ restrict to the Donaldson's structures on $\mathcal{AF}(S)$, while $\mathbb{I}, \mathbf i{\circ}\mathbb{J}, \mathbf{i}\circ\mathbb{K}$ restrict to $\mathbf{I}'$, $\mathbf{J}'$, $\mathbf{K}'$ from \cite{MazSepTamb}. Moreover, in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem: compatibility_omega_I} we showed that $\omega_{\mathbb{I}}$ restricts to $\omega_{\mathbf{I}}$ on the almost-Fuchsian locus, and this is sufficient to deduce that the metric $g$ and the other two symplectic forms $\omega_{\mathbb{J}}$ and $\omega_{\mathbb{K}}$ restrict to $\omega_{\mathbf{J}}$ and $\omega_{\mathbf{K}}$, thanks to formulas~\eqref{eq: g, omegaJ, omegaK}. This concludes the first item. Analogously, for the second item it suffices to prove that $\omega_{\mathbb{I}}$ restricts to the symplectic form $\omega_{\mathbf{I}'}$ on the locus $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$. To carry out the computation, similarly to Lemma~\ref{lem: compatibility_omega_I} we use the inclusion $\iota_{\mathbb{R}}$ introduced in diagram~\eqref{eq:comm diag MGH}. It suffices to evaluate
\[
(\pi_r^* \omega_G)\big((\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_2),(\dot\rho_1',\dot\rho_2')\big)+(\pi_l^*\omega_G)\big((\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_2),(\dot\rho_1',\dot\rho_2')\big) ,
\]
where $\dot{\rho}_i$ and $\dot{\rho}_i'$ are variations of representations into $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ for $i=1,2$.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
Therefore, we obtain that \begin{align*}
(\pi_r^* \omega_G)\big((\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_2),(\dot\rho_1',\dot\rho_2')\big)&+(\pi_l^*\omega_G)\big((\dot\rho_1,\dot\rho_2),(\dot\rho_1',\dot\rho_2')\big) = \\ &=\big(\omega_G^\mathbb R(\dot \rho_1,\dot\rho_1')+\omega_G^\mathbb R(\dot\rho_2,\dot\rho_2')\big) .
\end{align*} As a consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm: Thm C and Cor H} we deduce $\mathrm{hol}^*\big(\pi_r^*\omega_G+\pi_l^*\omega_G\big)|_{\mathcal{MGH}(S)}=\omega_{\mathbf I'}$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- defn-19: body_md -->
\label{def:complex biKahler}
Let $(\mathbb X,\mathbf j)$ be a complex manifold with integrable almost-complex structure $\mathbf{j}:T\mathbb X\to T\mathbb X$. A \emph{complex bi-K\"ahler structure} is the data of two tensors $\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{P} \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{C}}(T^{1,0}\mathbb X)$ and a complex Riemannian metric $g$ that satisfy the following properties:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathcal{I}^2 = -\mathcal{P}^2 = - \mathrm{Id}$ and $\mathcal{I}= - \mathbf{j} \circ \mathcal{P}$;
\item $\mathcal{I}$ and $\mathcal{P}$ are $\mathbf{j}$--holomorphic and integrable (that is, their Nijenhuis tensors $N_{\mathcal{I}}$ and $N_{\mathcal{P}}$ vanish identically on $T^{1,0} \mathbb{X}$);
\item the $(+1)$-- and $(-1)$--eigenspaces of $\mathcal{P}_x$ in $T^{1,0}_x \mathbb{X}$ have the same dimension for any $x \in \mathbb{X}$;
\item $g$ is $\mathbf{j}$--holomorphic and satisfies $g(\mathcal{P}\cdot,\mathcal{P}\cdot)=-g(\cdot,\cdot)$;
\item The pairing $\omega:=g(\mathcal{P}\cdot,\cdot)$ defines a symplectic form. \end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-19 -->
<!-- thm-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:loustau sanders}
The space $\mathcal{QF}(S)$ admits a $\mathrm{MCG}(S)$--invariant complex bi-K\"ahler metric $(g_{\mathcal{QF}},\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{QF}},\mathbb{I}_{\mathcal{QF}},\mathcal P)$, where:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{QF}}$ is equal to the pullback of the endomorphism $\mathbf i_{\mathcal T(S)}\times\mathbf i_{\mathcal T(\overline S)}$ of $T(\mathcal{T}(S)\times \mathcal{T}(\overline{S}))$ via the Bers' double uniformization map;
\item $\mathbb{I}_{\mathcal{QF}}$ and $\mathcal{P}$ are equal to the pullback of the endomorphisms $\mathbf i_{\mathcal T(S)}\times\mathbf i_{\mathcal T(S)}$ and $(\mathrm{Id},-\mathrm{Id})$ of $T^{1,0}(\mathcal{T}(S)\times \mathcal{T}(\overline{S}))$, respectively, via the Bers' double uniformization map (where the $(1,0)$--part is taken with respect to $\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{QF}}$);
\item The induced symplectic form $\omega_{\mathcal{QF}}$ coincides with the restriction on $\mathcal{QF}(S)$ of  Goldman's (complex) symplectic form on the character variety $\chi^{irr}\big(\pi_1(S),\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})\big)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-15 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rem: convention Loustau-Sanders}
In the original paper of Loustau--Sanders \cite{loustau-sanders}, the holomorphic Riemannian metric is defined as $\omega_G(\mathcal P\cdot, \cdot)$, hence it differs from \(g_{\mathcal{QF}}\) defined here by a sign.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- thm-16: body_md -->
\label{thm: restriction to quasi-Fuchsian}
The two complex structures $\mathbf i, \mathbb I$ and the symplectic form $\omega_\mathbb I$ defined on $\mathbb M_0(S)$ restrict to the triple $(\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{QF}},\mathbb I_{\mathcal{QF}},2\omega_G)$ on $\mathcal{QF}(S)$.
<!-- end thm-16 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
By what was explained at the beginning of the section, the space of quasi-Fuchsian representations
\(\mathcal{QF}(S)\)
is diffeomorphic to a submanifold of \(\mathbb{M}_0(S)\), realized as \[
\mathcal{T}(S)\times\mathcal{T}(\overline S)=\{[J_1,q_1,-J_2,\overline{q_2},u]\in\mathbb{M}_0(S)\mid q_1=q_2=u=0\}.
\] By the definition of the complex structure \(\mathbf{i}\) on $\mathbb M(S)$, when restricted to
\(T^{1,0}\mathcal{T}(S)\times T^{1,0}\mathcal{T}(\overline{S})\),
it acts by multiplication by \(i\) on both the Beltrami differential \(\dot{\mu}_1\) and the conjugate Beltrami differential \(\dot{\overline{\mu}}_2\). In other words, it coincides with the product complex structure
\(\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{T}(S)}\times\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{T}(\overline{S})}\).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
By point (1) of Theorem~\ref{thm:loustau sanders}, this latter complex structure is biholomorphic to \(\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{QF}}\) on $\mathcal{QF}(S)$. On the other hand, the endomorphism $\mathbb{I}$ defined in~\eqref{eq: def I in trivialization of pi} and~\eqref{eq: Complex structure I} restricts to \(T^{1,0}\mathcal{T}(S)\times T^{1,0}\mathcal{T}(\overline{S})\) and it acts as the multiplication by \(i\) on the Beltrami differential \(\dot{\mu}_1\) and by \(-i\) on the conjugate Beltrami differential \(\dot{\overline{\mu}}_2\). According to Theorem~\ref{thm:loustau sanders} point (2), its restriction coincides with $\mathbb{I}_{\mathcal{QF}}$ on $\mathcal{QF}(S)$. The final statement concerning the symplectic form $\omega_{\mathbb{I}}$ follows from its definition in~\eqref{eq: omega_mathbb I}, by a computation entirely analogous to that carried out in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem: compatibility_omega_I}, where in this case the inclusion at the level of representations is the diagonal embedding.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{cor: restriction of complex hyperkahler to QF(S)}
The complex hyperK\"ahler metric on $\mathbb M_0(S)$ extends the Loustau-Sanders complex bi-K\"ahler metric on $\mathcal{QF}(S)$, up to some constants. More precisely, the holomorphic Riemannian metric \(g\) restricts to $-2ig_{\mathcal{QF}}$.
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
The complex bi-K\"ahler structure on $\mathcal{QF}(S)$ (Theorem \ref{thm:loustau sanders}) is completely determined by the triple $(\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{QF}},\mathbb{I}_{\mathcal{QF}},\omega_G)$, since $\mathcal{P}=\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{QF}}\circ \mathbb{I}_{\mathcal{QF}}$ and $g_{\mathcal{QF}}=\omega_G(\mathcal{P}\cdot,\cdot)$. In particular, 
\begin{align*}
    g|_{\mathcal{QF}(S)}&=\omega_{\mathbb I}(\cdot,\mathbb I\cdot)|_{\mathcal{QF}(S)}  \\ &=2\omega_G(\cdot,\mathbb I_{\mathcal{QF}}\cdot) \tag{Theorem \ref{thm: restriction to quasi-Fuchsian}}  \\ &=-2\omega_G(\cdot,\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{QF}}\circ\mathcal P\cdot) \tag{Definition \ref{def:complex biKahler}}  \\ &=-2i\omega_G(\cdot,\mathcal P\cdot) \tag{$\omega_G$ is $\mathbf{i}_{\mathcal{QF}}$-holomorphic} \\ &=-2ig_{\mathcal{QF}}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lem-12: body_md -->
\label{lem: C* su mathbb M}
For every $\gamma_0$ in $\mathrm M^*(S)$, there exist open subsets $U\subset \mathrm M^*(S)$ and $V\subset \mathbb C^*$ with $\gamma_0\in U$ and $1\in V$ such that, if $\gamma_1, \gamma_2\in U$ are identified in $\mathbb M(S)$ and $\zeta\in V$, then $\zeta\cdot \gamma_1$ and $\zeta\cdot \gamma_2$ both lie in $\mathrm M^*(S)$ and are identified in $\mathbb M(S)$. 

Denoting by $[U]$ the image of $U$ through the projection $\mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathbb M(S)$, the induced maps 
\begin{align*}
    V\times U\to \mathrm M^*(S) &\qquad (\zeta, \gamma)\mapsto \zeta\cdot \gamma\\
    V\times [U]\to \mathbb M(S) & \qquad (\zeta, [\gamma])\mapsto [\zeta\cdot \gamma]
\end{align*}
are both holomorphic.
<!-- end lem-12 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Recall the commutative diagram in Equation \eqref{eq: diagramma proiezioni} and that $\pi$ and $\pi_0$ are local biholomorphisms. The $\mathbb C^*$ action on $\mathrm M(S)$ commutes through the projection $\mathrm M(S)\to \mathrm{QD}(S)\times \mathrm{QD}(\overline S)$ with the $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}^*$-action on $\mathrm{QD}(S)\times \mathrm{QD}(\overline S)$ given by $\zeta\cdot (c_1, \overline{c_2}, q_1, \overline{q_2})= (c_1, \overline{c_2}, \zeta q_1, \zeta^{-1}\overline{q_2})$; this action is trivially holomorphic and descends to a well-defined holomorphic action of $\mathbb C^*$ on $\mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)$. 

Now, since topologically we have $\mathrm{QD}(S)\times\mathrm{QD}(\overline S)\cong\mathbb{QD}(S)\times \mathbb{QD}(\overline S)\times \operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}_0(S)\times \operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}_0(S)$, every element in $\mathrm{QD}(S)\times\mathrm{QD}(\overline S)$ admits a complete system of neighborhoods such that the intersection with every $\operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}_0(S)\times \operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}_0(S)$-orbit is connected. Using this remark, together with the facts that $\pi$ and $\pi_0$ are local homeomorphisms and that the $\mathbb C^*$-action on $\mathrm M(S)$ is continuous, we can say that, for all element $\gamma_0\in \mathrm M^*(S)$, there exist $U$ and $U_0$ neighborhoods of $\gamma$ and $V\subset \mathbb C^*$ neighborhood of $1$ such that: \begin{itemize}
\item for all $\zeta\in V$ and $\gamma\in U$, $\zeta\cdot \gamma\in U_0$;
\item
the restrictions of $\pi_0$ on $U$ and $U_0$ and the restrictions of $\pi$ on $[U]$ and $[U_0]$ are all injective, hence biholomorphisms with their respective images;
    \item the intersection of $U$ with every fiber of the projection to $\mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathbb M(S)$ is connected.
\end{itemize}

Now, let $F$ be the intersection of $U$ with a fiber of $\mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathbb M(S)$. By construction of $\mathbb M(S)$, $[\pi_0(F)]\in \mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)$ is a point.  The assumption on $U$ implies that, for all $\zeta\in V$, $\zeta\cdot F\subset U_0$ is connected, and it is mapped through $[\pi_0]$ to the element $\zeta\cdot [\pi_0(F)]$. We therefore conclude that $[\zeta\cdot F]$ is one point in $\mathbb M(S)$. 

From the commutativity of the diagram
 \begin{center}
\label{eq: diagramma restrizioni}
   \begin{tikzcd}
 V\times U\arrow[r, "\mathit{action}"] \arrow[d, "\mathit{id}\times \pi_0"]  & U_0 \arrow[d, "\pi_0"]  \\
V\times \pi_0(U) \arrow[r, "\ \mathit{action}\ "] & \pi_0(U_0)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
we get that the top horizontal map is holomorphic as a consequence of the holomorphicity of the bottom one and of the fact that the vertical maps are biholomorphisms. Similarly for $V\times[U]\to [U_0]$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- prop-25: body_md -->
\label{prop: infintiesimal generator well-def}
    The derivative
    \[
   {\xi}|_{[\gamma]}:= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}z}\bigg|_{z=0} [e^{iz}\cdot \gamma]
    \]
provides a well-defined $\mathbf i$-holomorphic vector field on $\mathbb M(S)$, hence an element $\xi\in H^0(T^{1,0}(\mathbb M(S))$.
<!-- end prop-25 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem: C* su mathbb M}, for every element $\gamma_0\in \mathrm M_0(S)$ there exists a neigbourhood $U$ such that, for all $\gamma\in U$ with $[\gamma]=[\gamma_0]$, the maps $z\mapsto [e^{iz}\cdot \gamma]$ and $z\mapsto [e^{iz}\cdot \gamma_0]$, defined for sufficiently small $z\in \operatorname{\mathbb{C}}$, coincide and are holomorphic. Hence, they determine the same vector 
    $$
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}z}\bigg|_{z=0} [e^{iz}\cdot \gamma]\in T_{[\gamma]}^{1,0}\mathbb M(S)~.
    $$
    This defines a locally constant map from the fiber over $[\gamma]$ of $\mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathbb M(S)$ to $T_{[\gamma]}^{1,0}\mathbb M(S)$. Since the fibers are connected, we conclude that the map is well defined. 

    Finally, the holomorphicity in Lemma \ref{lem: C* su mathbb M} implies the holomorphicity of the vector field $\xi$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rmk: definition of infinitesimal tensors under C*}
Observe that $\xi\cdot \upalpha=0$ if and only if $(e^{-iz})^*\upalpha\equiv \upalpha$ on sufficiently small neighborhoods of any point in $\mathbb M(S)$ and for sufficiently small $|z|$. Indeed, in a local description, $\xi\cdot \upalpha=0$ implies that, for $z_0$ sufficiently small,
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}z}\bigg|_{z=z_0}  (e^{-{iz}})^*\upalpha = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}z}\bigg|_{z=z_0}  (e^{-iz_0})^* (e^{{-iz+iz_0}})^*\upalpha = (e^{-iz_0})^* (\xi\cdot \upalpha)=0,
\]
which means that, for small $z$, $(e^{-iz})^*\upalpha$ does not depend on $z$, hence $(e^{-iz})^*\upalpha\equiv \upalpha$.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- thm-17: body_md -->
\label{thm: circle action MGH}
The circle action on \(\mathcal{AF}(S)\) satisfies: \[\label{eq: relation for the circle action on AF} ({e^{i\theta}})^*\mathbf g=\mathbf g,\quad ({e^{i\theta}})^*\mathbf I=\mathbf I,\quad ({e^{i\theta}})^*\omega_{\mathbf I}=\omega_\mathbf {I}. 
\]
Similarly, the circle action on $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ satisfies:
 \[\label{eq: relation for the circle action on MGH} ({e^{i\theta}})^*\mathbf g'=\mathbf g',\quad ({e^{i\theta}})^*\mathbf I'=\mathbf I',\quad ({e^{i\theta}})^*\omega_{\mathbf I'}=\omega_\mathbf {I'}. 
\]
<!-- end thm-17 -->
<!-- thm-18: body_md -->
\label{thm: C* action on M0(S)}
Recall the tensors $g, \mathbb I,$ and $\omega_{\mathbb I}$ from the complex hyperKähler structure of $\mathbb M_0(S)$. Then,
\[
\xi\cdot g =0, \qquad\qquad \xi\cdot \mathbb I= 0, \qquad\qquad \xi\cdot \omega_{\mathbb I}=0.
\]
<!-- end thm-18 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Let $\gamma \in \mathrm{MGH}(S)$ (see Equation \eqref{eq:inclusion MGH in M}).
By Theorem \ref{thm: circle action MGH} and the third item of Theorem \ref{thm:main}, we know that, at $[\gamma]$ we have the identities 
\[\xi\cdot g |_{[\gamma]}= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}z} \bigg|_{z=0} (e^{iz})^* g = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\bigg|_{\theta=0} (e^{i\theta})^*g= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\bigg|_{\theta=0} (e^{i\theta})^*\mathbf g'= 0
\]
and similar for $\mathbb I$ and $\omega_{\mathbb I}$. Since they are holomorphic tensors that vanish along $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$, a totally real submanifold of maximal dimension, they vanish on the whole $\mathbb M_0(S)$ (Lemma \ref{lem: fundamental lem analytic continuation} and Remark \ref{rmk: fundamental_lemma_applied to tensors}).
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- thm-19: body_md -->
\label{thm: hamiltonian MGH}
The circle action on \(\mathcal{AF}(S)\) (resp. \(\mathcal{MGH}(S)\)) is Hamiltonian with respect to \(\omega_{\mathbf I}\) (resp. \(\omega_{\mathbf I'}\)), with Hamiltonian function given by the area functional, assigning to each equivariant minimal (resp. maximal) immersion the area of the first fundamental form, seen as a Riemannian metric on $S$.
<!-- end thm-19 -->
<!-- lem-13: body_md -->
\label{lem: Area functional on M*(S) is holomorphic}
The complex area functional \(\hat{\mathcal A}:\mathrm{M}^*(S)\to\mathbb C\) is holomorphic.
<!-- end lem-13 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
We will prove the stronger statement that the map
\[
    \mathrm{M}^*(S) \longrightarrow \Omega^2(S,\mathbb C),
    \qquad
    \gamma \longmapsto \mathrm{d}A_{\mathtt{I}_\gamma},
\]
is holomorphic.

We first consider finite-dimensional families. Let $\Lambda$ be a
finite-dimensional smooth manifold and let
$\lambda \mapsto \gamma_\lambda \in \mathrm{M}^*(S)$ be a smooth map.
Set
\[
    \mathtt{I}_\lambda := \mathtt{I}_{\gamma_\lambda},
    \qquad
    \mathcal J_\lambda := \mathcal J_{\gamma_\lambda},
    \qquad
    \omega_\lambda := \mathrm{d}A_{\mathtt{I}_\lambda}
    = \mathtt{I}_\lambda(\mathcal J_\lambda\,\cdot,\cdot).
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem: from M* to I II}, the tensor $\mathtt{I}_\lambda$ depends smoothly on $(\lambda,p)\in\Lambda\times S$.

The same is true of $\mathcal J_\lambda$ and $\omega_\lambda$.
Indeed, the two isotropic lines of $\mathtt{I}_\lambda$ are distinct
roots of the quadratic equation
$\mathtt{I}_\lambda(v,v)=0$ in the projective tangent space, and
therefore vary smoothly with $(\lambda,p)$.
Since $\mathtt{I}_\lambda$ is positive, these lines lie in distinct
components of $\mathbb P_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C T_pS) \setminus \mathbb P_{\mathbb R}(T_pS)$, and the orientation of $S$ consistently distinguishes them. Since these lines depend smoothly on $\lambda$, also the tensor $\mathcal J_{\lambda}$, defined as $i$ on one line and $-i$ on the other one, depends smoothly on $\lambda$. 

Suppose now that $\Lambda$ is a complex manifold and that
$\lambda\mapsto\gamma_\lambda$ is holomorphic.
Fix a complex structure $J_0$ compatible with the orientation
of $S$, and let $z$ be a local $J_0$-holomorphic coordinate
on an open subset $U\subset S$. 
Keeping this coordinate fixed as $\lambda$ varies, write
\[
    \mathtt{I}_\lambda
    =
    E_\lambda\,\mathrm{d}z\otimes \mathrm{d}z
    +F_\lambda
       \bigl(\mathrm{d}z\otimes \mathrm{d}\bar z+\mathrm{d}\bar z\otimes \mathrm{d}z\bigr)
    +G_\lambda\,\mathrm{d}\bar z\otimes \mathrm{d}\bar z,
    \qquad
    \omega_\lambda=a_\lambda\,\mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z.
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem: from M* to I II}, the coefficients $E_\lambda,F_\lambda,G_\lambda$
are holomorphic in $\lambda$ at every point of $U$, since
the frame $(\partial_z,\partial_{\bar z})$ is independent
of $\lambda$. By a standard computation, we have $    a_\lambda^2=E_\lambda G_\lambda-F_\lambda^2$,
thus the area form $\omega_\lambda$ depends holomorphically on $\lambda$ at each point of $S$, as well. Together with smoothness in $(\lambda,p)$, this shows that
\[
    \Lambda\longrightarrow\Omega^2(S,\mathbb C),
    \qquad
    \lambda\longmapsto\omega_\lambda,
\]
is holomorphic.

We now pass to the Fr\'echet setting.
The argument above, applied to smooth curves,
shows that the map
$\gamma\mapsto \mathrm{d}A_{\mathtt{I}_\gamma}$
maps smooth curves to smooth curves in $\Omega^2(S,\mathbb C)$.
It is therefore smooth by Theorem \ref{thm: boman}.
Moreover, its restriction to every holomorphic disk is holomorphic
by the preceding computation, thus its differential is
$\mathbb C$-linear.
Hence $\gamma\mapsto \mathrm{d}A_{\mathtt{I}_\gamma}$ is holomorphic.

Finally, integration over $S$ defines a continuous
$\mathbb C$-linear map $\Omega^2(S,\mathbb C)\rightarrow\mathbb C$,
therefore
\[
    \widehat{\mathcal A}(\gamma)
    =\int_S \mathrm{d}A_{\mathtt{I}_\gamma}
\]
is holomorphic.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- prop-26: body_md -->
\label{prop:area functional well defined}
The complex area functional descends to the complex manifold \(\mathbb M(S)\), thereby defining a holomorphic function
\[
\mathcal A:\mathbb M(S)\longrightarrow\mathbb C.
\]
<!-- end prop-26 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
First, observe that \(\hat{\mathcal A}\) is invariant under the action of \(\operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}_0(S)\).  Indeed, for every \(\varphi\in\operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}_0(S)\), one has \( \mathtt I_{\varphi^*\gamma}=\varphi^*\mathtt I_\gamma \) and consequently \( \mathrm{d}A_{\mathtt I_{\varphi^*\gamma}} = \varphi^*\mathrm{d}A_{\mathtt I_\gamma}. \) Given that \(\varphi\) is orientation-preserving, it follows that \( \hat{\mathcal A}(\varphi^*\gamma)= \hat{\mathcal A}(\gamma).\) As a consequence of the \(\mathrm{Diff}_0(S)\)-invariance and Lemma~\ref{lem: invariance of map under Diff-action}, the functional \(\hat{\mathcal A}\) descends to a well-defined holomorphic function \(\mathcal A:\mathbb M(S)\longrightarrow\mathbb C.\)
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- thm-20: body_md -->
The following identity holds on $\mathbb M_0(S)$:
\[
\mathrm{d}\mathcal A= \omega_{\mathbb I}(\xi, \cdot) 
\]
<!-- end thm-20 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Both terms in the equality are holomorphic 1-forms, so it suffices to show that they coincide along the totally real submanifold $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$. This is indeed the case: along $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$, $\mathcal A$ restricts to the usual area functional, $\xi$ corresponds to $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta} e^{i\theta}$, and $\omega_{\mathbb I}$ restricts to $\omega_{\mathbf I'}$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- prop-27: body_md -->
\label{prop: totally geodesic holomorphic metric}
Let $(\mathbb{X}, \mathbf{i})$ be a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$, equipped with a holomorphic Riemannian metric $g$. Let $N\subset \mathbb{X}$ be a maximal totally real submanifold and assume that the restriction $g|_{TN}$
is real-valued and non-degenerate. Then $N$ is a totally geodesic sumbanifold of $\mathbb{X}$.
<!-- end prop-27 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Denote $h=g|_{TN}$. Let $D$ denote the holomorphic Levi-Civita connection of $g$. Recall that, according to Definition~\ref{def:homorphic levi-civita}, $D$ is the $\mathbb{C}$-linear extension of an affine connection of $\mathbb{X}$. In particular, $D_V$ keeps the real tangent bundle $T \mathbb{X}$ invariant whenever $V \in \Gamma(T \mathbb{X})$. As in the classical Riemannian setting, the submanifold $N$ is totally geodesic if and only if, for any pair of tangent vector fields $X, Y \in \Gamma(T N)$, $D_X Y$ is tangent to $N$. Since $N$ is maximal totally real, for every $p\in N$ one has a direct sum decomposition $T_p\mathbb{X}=T_pN\oplus \mathbf{i}(T_pN)$ as real vector spaces (see Definition \ref{def: totally real submanifold}).
Let $X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields tangent to $N$. The Koszul formula gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2g(D_XY,Z) = & \, X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr) + Y\bigl(g(X,Z)\bigr) - Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)\\
& + g([X,Y],Z) - g([X,Z],Y) - g([Y,Z],X) .
\end{aligned}
\]
Every term on the right-hand side is real along $N$. Hence $g(D_XY,Z)\in\mathbb R$ for every vector field $Z$ tangent to $N$.
Fix $p\in N$ and write $D_XY=A+\mathbf{i}B$, for some $A,B\in T_pN$. Since $g$ is complex bilinear,
\[
g(D_XY,Z)=h(A,Z)+i\,h(B,Z)
\]
for every $Z\in T_pN$. The left-hand side is real, so $h(B,Z)=0$
for every $Z\in T_pN$. Since by assumption $h$ is non-degenerate, we conclude that $B=0$ and, hence, $D_XY\in T_pN$. Since $p \in N$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $D_X Y$ is tangent to $N$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- cor-5: body_md -->
The submanifolds $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ are both totally geodesic in $(\mathbb M_0(S),g)$. Since their intersection coincides with the Teichmüller
space $\mathcal T(S)$, the latter is also totally geodesic in $(\mathbb M_0(S),g)$.
<!-- end cor-5 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
By Corollary~\ref{cor: restriction of complex hyperkahler to AF e MSH}, the holomorphic metric \(g\) restricts to \(\mathbf g\) on \(\mathcal{AF}(S)\) and to \(\mathbf g'\) on \(\mathcal{MGH}(S)\), and both restricted metrics are real and non-degenerate. Moreover, Proposition~\ref{prop: AF and MGH are totally real submanifolds} shows that both spaces are totally real submanifolds of maximal dimension. The first part of the statement therefore follows from Proposition~\ref{prop: totally geodesic holomorphic metric}. As for the second part, Theorem~\ref{thm:hyperkahler_almost_fuchsian} implies, for instance, that \(\mathcal{T}(S)\) is totally geodesic in \(\mathcal{AF}(S)\). The desired conclusion then follows.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- cor-6: body_md -->
The quasi-Fuchsian space \(\mathcal{QF}(S)\) is a totally geodesic submanifold of \(\big(\mathbb M_0(S),g\big)\).
<!-- end cor-6 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Consider any point $[\gamma_0]$ in $\mathcal{QF}(S)$ and take a neighborhood $W_0$ inside $\mathbb M_0(S)$ over which the projection $\pi$ to $\mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)$ gives a homeomorphism with the image. Up to shrinking it, we can assume that an element $[\gamma]\in W_0$ lies in $\mathcal {QF}(S)$ if and only if $\pi([\gamma])$ lies in the zero section $\mathcal T(S)\times \mathcal T(\overline S)\subset\mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)$.

    
    By Lemma \ref{lem: C* su mathbb M}, there exists $\operatorname{\varepsilon}>0$ and a smaller neighborhood $W\subset W_0$ of $[\gamma]$ such that, for all $|z|<\operatorname{\varepsilon}$, the action times $e^{iz}$ can be seen as a map from $W$ to $W_0$.
    By Theorem \ref{thm: C* action on M0(S)} and by Remark \ref{rmk: definition of infinitesimal tensors under C*}, we have that $(e^{-iz})^*g=g$ on $W$, hence every $e^{-iz}$ determines locally an isometry with the image. On the other hand, since $\pi$ conjugates the $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}^*$-actions, an element $[\gamma]$ in $W$ is fixed by $e^{-iz}$ for all $|z|<\operatorname{\varepsilon}$ if and only if $\pi([\gamma])\in \mathcal T(S)\times \mathcal T(\overline S)$, hence if and only if $[\gamma]\in W_0\cap \mathcal{QF}(S)$.
By a standard argument (e.g. see  \cite[Chapter~II, Theorem~5.1]{kobayashi2012transformation}), every geodesic tangent to $\mathcal{QF}(S)$ starting at $[\gamma_0]$ is then preserved by the action times each $e^{iz}$, hence it is contained inside $\mathcal{QF}(S)$, proving that $\mathcal{QF}(S)$ is totally geodesic.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rmk:holo involution}
   Similarly to the proof that $\mathcal{QF}(S)$ is totally geodesic as a fixed point of an isometric, holomorphic action, also  $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ can be realized as fixed loci of a local \emph{antiholomorphic} involution. To see this, observe that the involutions of $\mathrm M(S)$ given by
     \begin{align*}
       \nu\colon (J_1, q_1, -J_2, \overline{q_2}, u)&\mapsto (J_2, q_2, -J_1, \overline{q_1}, \overline u)\qquad \text{and}\\
       \nu'\colon (J_1, q_1, -J_2, \overline{q_2}, u)&\mapsto (J_2, -q_2, -J_1, -\overline{q_1}, \overline u) \ ,
   \end{align*}   
 fix pointwise $\mathrm{AF}(S)$ and $\mathrm{MGH}(S)$ respectively. 
These involutions descend to suitable neighborhoods of $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ in $\mathbb M_0(S)$ that project injectively to $\mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)$, over which they correspond to $ [J_1, q_1, -J_2, \overline{q_2}]\mapsto [J_2, \pm q_2, -J_1, \pm \overline{q_1}]$, hence they are antiholomorphic involutions. By an analytic continuation argument, using that the restriction of $g$ to $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ is real, one can show that these involutions pull-back the metric $g$ to its complex conjugate, hence they are isometries for the real part of $g$; as a consequence, one could deduce by an alternative argument that $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ are totally geodesic.

We actually expect $\nu$ and $\nu'$ to descend to global anti-holomorphic maps on $\mathbb M(S)$. However, although it is easily verified that $\nu$ and $\nu'$ preserve the infinitesimal rigidity, it is less evident that they preserve  the condition for which the holonomy lies in $\chi^*(\pi_1(S), \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})^2)$.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{rmk:constant curvature surfaces}
    The above definition is inspired by the  construction of equidistant surfaces in the Anti-de Sitter space (\cite{kirill07}, see also \cite{barbot2011, bonsante-seppi2018}). To explain this, assume here that $\sigma$ is an immersion in $\mathbb{A}\mathrm{d}\mathbb{S}^3\cong \mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)$, seen as a totally geodesic subspace of $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$. Then $\sigma$ has a  normal vector field in $\mathbb{A}\mathrm{d}\mathbb{S}^3$ of norm identically $-1$. The normal vector field $N$ in $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ is defined by the condition $\langle N, N\rangle =1$, so it equals $\pm i$ times the $\mathbb{A}\mathrm{d}\mathbb{S}^3$ normal vector field. Therefore $\sigma_{\pm}'$ are obtained as exponential maps \emph{inside} $\mathbb{A}\mathrm{d}\mathbb{S}^3$, and this recovers the construction in \cite{kirill07}.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- prop-28: body_md -->
In the notations above, 
\[
\mathtt I'_{\pm}:=(\sigma_{\pm}')^*\operatorname{\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle}_{\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})} =  \frac 12 \mathtt I ((id\mp iB)\cdot , (id\mp iB)\cdot).
\]
In particular,  $\mathtt I'_{\pm}$ is a complex metric if and only if $\mathrm K^{\mathtt I}$ vanishes nowhere. When this happens, $\mathtt I'_{\pm}$ both have constant curvature $-2$.
<!-- end prop-28 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Differentiating the expression for $\sigma_{\pm}$, we have that
\begin{align*}
\mathtt I'_{\pm} =& \langle{\mathrm{d}\sigma_{\pm}, \mathrm{d}\sigma_{\pm}}\rangle= \frac 12 \langle{\mathrm{d}\sigma \pm i dN, \mathrm{d}\sigma \pm i dN}\rangle=\\
=&\frac 12 \langle{\mathrm{d}\sigma \mp \mathrm{d}\sigma\circ (iB), \mathrm{d}\sigma \mp \mathrm{d}\sigma\circ (iB) }\rangle= \\
=&\frac 12 \mathtt I( id\mp iB, id\mp iB).
\end{align*}
For the second part of the statement, just observe that, by the Gauss equation~\eqref{eq: Gauss PSL(2,C)}, $\mathtt I'_{\pm}$ is a complex metric if and only if $$0\ne \det(id\pm iB) =1-\det(B) = -\mathrm K^{\mathtt I}.$$ Since $id\pm iB$ is Codazzi for $\mathtt I$, $\det(id\pm iB)\ne 0$ implies that the Levi-Civita connection for $\mathtt I'_{\pm}$ is given by $$\nabla^{\mathtt I'_{\pm}}_X Y= (id\pm iB)^{-1}  (\nabla^{\mathtt I}_X ( (id\pm iB)(Y) ) ). $$
Hence, by a standard computation (see for instance the proof of \cite[Proposition 3.9]{ElE}), one  gets that
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
    $$\mathrm K^{\mathtt I_{\pm}'} =2\frac{K_{\mathtt I}}{\det(id\pm iB)} = 2\frac{-1+\det(B)}{1-\det(B)}=-2. $$
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
Observe that $\mathrm W(S)$ contains $\mathrm{MGH}(S)$: if $\gamma\in\mathrm{MGH}(S) $ then $\mathtt I'_{\pm}$ are hyperbolic Riemannian metrics, which are Bers metrics.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- lem-14: body_md -->
The space $\mathrm{AF}(S)$ is contained in $\mathrm W(S)$.
<!-- end lem-14 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Let $\gamma=(J,q,-J, \overline q, u)\in \mathrm{AF}(S)$, let  $z$ be a local holomorphic coordinate for $J$ and write $q=\operatorname{\varphi} \mathrm{d}z^2$ and $h=\lambda \mathrm{d}z\mathrm{d}\overline z$ for the hyperbolic metric conformal to $J$. Then, the isotropic directions of $\mathtt I'_{\pm}$ are given by the complex lines generated by \[
    X_{\pm}= \partial_z \pm \frac{\operatorname{\varphi}}{e^{2u}\lambda}\partial_{\overline z} \qquad \text{and} \qquad  Y_{\pm}=\partial_{\overline z} \pm \frac{\overline{\operatorname{\varphi}}}{e^{2u}\lambda}\partial_{ z}.
    \]
    A simple computation shows that a vector $\alpha \partial_z+\beta\partial_{\overline z}\ne 0$ determines a point in a connected component of $\mathbb P(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)\setminus \mathbb P(TS)$ according to the sign of $Re(\frac{\alpha-\beta}{\alpha+\beta})$ or equivalently of $Re(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha-\beta})$ (or just one of the two when the other is not defined). In our setting, it is straightforward to check that $$\frac{\operatorname{\varphi}\overline{\operatorname{\varphi}}}{e^{4u}\lambda^2}<1 $$ implies that $X_{\pm}$ and $Y_{\pm}$ lie in opposite connected components, implying that $\mathtt I'_{\pm}$ are both positive complex metrics. Finally, $\mathrm{AF}(S)$ is connected, $\mathtt I'_{\pm}$ is clearly a Bers metric when $q=0$, and Bers metrics are connected components of the space of positive complex metrics of curvature $-1$: we conclude that $2\mathtt I'_\pm$ are both Bers metrics.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lem-15: body_md -->
\label{lem: Theta holomorphic}
    There exists an open connected subset $\mathbb W(S)\subset \mathbb M_0(S)$ containing both $\mathcal{AF}(S)$ and $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ such that $\widehat \Theta$ descends to a holomorphic map
    \[
    \Theta\colon \big(\mathbb W(S),\mathbf i\big) \to  \big(\mathcal{QF}(S)\times \mathcal{QF}(S), (J_\chi,J_\chi)\big),
    \]
 namely $\Theta([\gamma])=\widehat\Theta(\gamma)$ for an open subset of representatives $\gamma$ of $[\gamma]$.
<!-- end lem-15 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Denote $Z= \mathrm{AF}(S)\cup \mathrm{MGH}(S)$ and $\mathcal Z=\mathcal{AF}(S)\cup \mathcal{MGH}(S)\subset \mathbb M(S)$. 

Since $\widehat \Theta$ is $\mathrm{Diff}_0(S)$--invariant, it is constant within each fiber of the projection ${Z}\to \mathcal Z$, defining continuously the map $\Theta$ on $Z$.
Moreover, since $\widehat \Theta$ is also holomorphic, we get that, for all $\gamma\in \mathrm W(S)$ and $X\in \Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} TS)$, 
$$
\mathrm{d}\widehat \Theta(\mathscr L_X\gamma)=\mathrm{d}\widehat \Theta(\mathscr L_{Re (X)}\gamma)+i \mathrm{d}\widehat \Theta(\mathscr L_{Im (X)}\gamma)= 0~.
$$ 
Hence, by Proposition \ref{prop: tangent fiber M*}, $\mathrm{d}\widehat \Theta$ is constantly zero on the kernel of the differential map of the projection $ \mathrm W(S)\to \mathbb M(S)$.

Since the map $\pi\colon \mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathrm{QD}(S)\times\mathrm{QD}(S)$ is a local biholomorphism, for all $\gamma$ in $\mathrm Z$ we can find a neighborhood $U\subset \mathrm W(S)$ such that the fibers of the projection $p\colon \mathrm U\to \mathbb M(S)$ are connected. The map $\widehat \Theta|_{U}$ is therefore constant among the fibers of $U\to \mathbb M(S)$, hence $\widehat \Theta|_U$ descends to a well-defined map $\Theta$ in a neighborhood of $[\gamma]$.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
It is simple to check that this local definition of $\Theta$ is holomorphic. Indeed, using the local biholomorphisms $\mathrm M^*(S)\to \mathrm{QD}(S)\times  \mathrm{QD}(\overline S)$ and $\mathbb M(S)\to \mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)$, we can construct local charts for $\mathrm M^*(S)$ of the form by $U_1\times U_2$ with $U_1\subset \mathbb{M}(S)$ and $U_2\subset \mathrm{Diff}_0(S)\times \mathrm{Diff}_0(S)$, over which $\widehat \Theta(u_1,u_2)= \Theta(u_1)$: the holomorphicity of $\Theta$ then follows by the holomorphicity of $\widehat \Theta$.

We are left to prove that these local descriptions of $\Theta$ along $Z$ match. This follows from a variation of standard topological argument (see the proof of Theorem 6.20 in \cite{ESrank2}, or the suggested proof for the \emph{Generalized inverse function theorem} in Exercise 1.8.14 in \cite{GuillPoll} and \cite{GIFT}).

Let $m$ be a Riemannian metric on a neighborhood of $\mathcal Z$ inside $\mathbb M(S)$ such that $\mathcal Z_1:=\mathcal{AF}(S)$, $\mathcal Z_2:=\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ and $\mathcal Z_3:=\mathcal{AF}(S)\cap \mathcal{MGH}(S)$ are all totally geodesic. This can be done for instance by restricting $\pi$ a global biholomorphism from a neighborhood of $\mathcal Z$ inside $\mathbb M(S)$ to an open subset of $\mathbb{QD}(S)\times\mathbb{QD}(\overline S)$ as in Theorem 6.20 in \cite{ESrank2}, and by pulling back a product metric coming from a Riemannian metric on $\mathbb{QD}(S)$ for which $[c,q]\mapsto [c,-q]$ is an isometry. 

For each $\mathcal Z_i$, one can construct a locally finite cover $\{V_i^j\}$ of open subsets of $\mathbb M(S)$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
    \item the construction above defines, on each $V_i^j$, a local holomorphic extension $\Theta_i^j$ coinciding with $\Theta|_{\mathcal Z_i}$ on $V_i^j\cap \mathcal Z_i$,
    \item each $\overline {V_i^j}$ is a geodesically convex ball,
    \item every point of $V_i^j$ has a unique closest point projection to $\mathcal Z_i$, with the segment realizing the distance being contained in $V_i^j$.
\end{itemize} 
With these assumptions, it is clear that $V_i^j$ and $V_i^k$ intersect if and only if $V_i^j\cap V_i^k\cap \mathcal Z_i$ is connected and nonempty, therefore $\Theta_i^j$ and $\Theta_i^k$ coincide on $V_i^j\cap V_i^k$ by uniqueness of the holomorphic continuation of $\Theta|_{\mathcal Z_i}$. As a result, we obtain a globally defined $\Theta_i$ on the open subset $\mathbb W_i=\cup_j V_i^j$.

Finally, up to shrinking the $\mathbb W_i$'s, we can assume that $\mathbb W_1\cap \mathbb W_2= \mathbb W_3$. Clearly, $\Theta_1$ and $\Theta_3$ must coincide on $\mathbb W_3$ by uniqueness of the complex analytic extension on $\mathbb W_3\cap \mathcal Z_1$. By applying the same argument for $\mathbb W_2\cap \mathbb W_3$, we get that on $\mathbb W(S):=\mathbb W_1\cup \mathbb W_2$ we can define $\Theta=\Theta_1\cup \Theta_2$.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- thm-21: body_md -->
\label{prop: iK on W_0}
On the open subset $\mathbb W(S)\subset\mathbb M_0(S)$, the tensor $\mathbb K$ coincides with $\Theta^*(-J_\chi,J_\chi)$.
<!-- end thm-21 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
By construction and by Proposition~\ref{prop: restriction of K} the tensor \(\mathbf i\circ\mathbb K\) is holomorphic on \(\mathbb{W}_0(S)\) and its restriction to \(\mathcal{MGH}(S)\) is equal to \(\mathbf{K}'\). Since the tensor \(\mathbf i\circ\Theta^*(-J_\chi,J_\chi)\) is also holomorphic on \(\mathbb{W}_0(S)\), if we show that its restriction to the anti-de Sitter locus coincides with \(\mathbf{K}'\), then we conclude by the analytic continuation argument (Lemma~\ref{lem: fundamental lem analytic continuation}). This follows from the following chain of equalities:
\begin{align*}
   \mathbf i\circ\Theta(-J_\chi,J_\chi)|_{\mathcal{MGH}(S)}&= \Theta^*(J_\chi,J_\chi)\circ\Theta^*(-J_\chi,J_\chi)|_{\mathcal{MGH}(S)} \tag{Lemma \ref{lem: Theta holomorphic}} \\ & =\Theta^*(\mathrm{Id},-\mathrm{Id})|_{\mathcal{MGH}(S)} \\ &=\mathcal{C}^*(\mathrm{Id},-\mathrm{Id}) \tag{Remark \ref{rmk:constant curvature surfaces}} \\ &=\mathbf{K}' \ . \tag{\cite[Theorem D]{MazSepTamb}}
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- defn-20: body_md -->
A \emph{bi-holomorphic manifold} is a triple $(M, \mathbf{i},\mathbf{P})$, where $(M, \mathbf{i})$ is a complex manifold and $\mathbf{P}$ is a holomorphic integrable para-complex structure.
<!-- end defn-20 -->
<!-- defn-21: body_md -->
\label{def:bicomplex_sympl} Let $(M,\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{P})$ be a bi-holomorphic manifold. A \emph{bi-holomorphic symplectic form} on $M$ is a $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}_{\tau}$--valued $2$--form $ \Omega=\Omega_{1}+\tau \Omega_{2}$ that is non-degenerate on $T^{1,0}_{+}M$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\Omega(X,\mathbf{i}Y)=\Omega(\mathbf{i}X,Y)=i\Omega(X,Y)$ for all bi-complex vector fields $X$ and $Y$;
    \item $\Omega(X,\mathbf{P}Y)=\Omega(\mathbf{P}X,Y)=\tau\Omega(X,Y)$ for all bi-complex vector fields $X$ and $Y$;
    \item $\mathrm{d} \Omega=0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defn-21 -->
<!-- thm-22: body_md -->
Goldman's symplectic form on $\chi^*(S,G_{\tau})$ is bi-holomorphic.
<!-- end thm-22 -->
<!-- thm-23: body_md -->
\label{thm: bi-complex reinterpretations} On $\mathbb M_0(S)$ we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hol_omega_g_tau}
    2\mathrm{hol}^{*}\omega_{G_{\tau}}=\omega_{\mathbb{I}}+i\tau\omega_{\mathbb{K}},  
\end{equation}
hence $\mathrm{hol}^{*}\omega_{G_{\tau}}$ is bi-holomorphic with respect to $(\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{i}\circ\mathbb{J})$. Moreover, on the open subset $\mathbb W_0(S)\subset\mathbb M_0(S)$ of Theorem~\ref{prop: iK on W_0}, the following identity holds
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Theta_omega_G_tau}
    2\Theta^{*}\omega_{G_{\tau}}=\omega_{\mathbb{I}}+i\tau\omega_{\mathbb{J}}. 
\end{equation}
In particular, $\Theta^{*}\omega_{G_{\tau}}$ is bi-holomorphic with respect to $(\mathbf{i}, -\mathbf{i}\circ\mathbb{K})$.
<!-- end thm-23 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Equation (\ref{eq:hol_omega_g_tau}) follows immediately combining Equation~\eqref{eq:omega_G_tau} with our definition of $\omega_{\mathbb{I}}$ in~\eqref{eq: omega_mathbb I} and Proposition~\ref{prop: formula for omega_K}. The right-hand side is bi-holomorphic with respect to $(\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{i}\circ\mathbb{J})$. \\
Equation~\eqref{eq:Theta_omega_G_tau} holds on the maximal totally real submanifold $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$ by \cite[Theorem D]{MazSepTamb}, hence it is true everywhere on the open subset $\mathbb W_0(S)\subset\mathbb M_0(S)$ which contains $\mathcal{MGH}(S)$. Again, the right-hand side is manifestly bi-holomorphic with respect to $(\mathbf{i}, -\mathbf{i}\circ\mathbb{K})$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- defn-22: body_md -->
\label{def: totally real submanifold} Let $(\mathbb X,\mathbf i)$ be a complex manifold. A real submanifold $Z\subset \mathbb X$ is said to be \emph{totally real} if \[ T_xZ\cap \mathbf i(T_xZ)=\{0\} \] for every $x\in Z$. It is said to be \emph{totally real of full dimension} (or \emph{maximal totally real}) if, in addition, \( \dim_{\mathbb R}Z=\dim_{\mathbb C}\mathbb X. \) Equivalently, in this case, \[ T_x\mathbb X=T_xZ\oplus \mathbf i(T_xZ) \] as real vector spaces, for every $x\in Z$.
<!-- end defn-22 -->
<!-- lem-16: body_md -->
\label{lem: fundamental lem analytic continuation}
    Let $\mathbb M$ and $\mathbb N$ be complex manifolds with $\mathbb M$ connected, and let $Z\subset \mathbb M$ be a totally real submanifold of full dimension ($\text{dim}_\mathbb R Z=\text{dim}_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}\mathbb{M}$). If $f_1, f_2\colon \mathbb M\to \mathbb N$ are holomorphic maps that coincide along $Z$, then they coincide everywhere.
<!-- end lem-16 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
By complex analiticity, it is sufficient to prove that if $f_1$ and $f_2$ coincide on an open subset of $\mathbb M$, then they coincide everywhere because $\mathbb M$ is connected. Fix a point $x\in Z$ and, up to composing with local charts around $x$, see $f_1, f_2$ as holomorphic maps between open subsets $\mathbb C^m\supset U\to V\subset \mathbb  C^n$, and see $Z\cap U$ as a totally real submanifold of $U$. 
    
   It is now simple to check that $f_1$ and $f_2$ have the same power series in the point $x\in U$. Let $X_1, \dots X_m $ be a local frame of linearly independent vector fields on $Z$ in a neighbrohood of $x$ that, up to shrinking the chart, we can assume to be the whole $U\cap Z$. On $U\cap Z$, we clearly have that $\partial_{X_k} f_1 =\partial_{X_k}f_2$, hence, by holomorphicity of $f_1$ and $f_2$, we also have that $\partial_{\mathbf J X_k} f_1 =i\partial_{X_k} f_1 =i \partial_{X_k}f_2 =\partial_{\mathbf JX_k}f_2$: as a consequence, in every point of $U\cap Z$, the maps $f_1$ and $f_2$ have the same 1-jet as functions on $U$. In particular the first order partial derivatives $\partial_{z_k} f_j$ induced by the holomorphic coordinates $(z_1, \dots, z_n)$ of $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}^n$ coincide on $U'\cap Z$ for $j=1$ and $j=2$. Applying the same argument by induction on $k$ to the holomorphic functions $\partial^k_{z_{i_1}, \dots, z_{i_k}} f_1$ and $\partial^k_{z_{i_1}, \dots, z_{i_k}} f_2$, we conclude that $f_1$ and $f_2$ share the same partial derivatives of any order in $x$. As a consequence, their power series at $x$ have the same coefficients, hence $f_1$ and $f_2$ coincide in an open neighborhood of $x$ inside $\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}^n$.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
\label{rmk: fundamental_lemma_applied to tensors} The same argument applies to holomorphic sections of a holomorphic vector bundle. Indeed, after choosing a local holomorphic trivialization, the claim reduces component-wise to Lemma~\ref{lem: fundamental lem analytic continuation}. Consequently, two holomorphic tensors on $\mathbb M$ that coincide along $Z$ must coincide everywhere on $\mathbb M$.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- lem-17: body_md -->
\label{lemma: formula variation H}
    Let $\Sigma$ be an oriented surface, let $\sigma:\Sigma\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ be an admissible minimal immersion in $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$, let $f\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$  and set $$\sigma_t(p):=\exp_{\sigma(p)}(tf(p)N(p))~.$$
    Then, if $H_\sigma$ denotes the mean curvature of $\sigma$, then
  
    $$\left. \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \right|_{t=0} H_\sigma =\Delta_{I}f +(\tr(B^ 2)-2)f$$
    where $\mathtt I$ denotes the complex first fundamental form of $\sigma$ and $B$ the complex shape operator.
<!-- end lem-17 -->
<!-- lem-18: body_md -->
Let $d$ denote the flat connection of the vector space $\mathrm{Mat}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$, and $D$ denote the holomorphic Levi-Civita connection of $\operatorname{\mathrm{SL}}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$. Given $A$ in $\operatorname{\mathrm{SL}}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ and two vector fields $X,Y$ on $\operatorname{\mathrm{SL}}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$, 
    \begin{equation} \label{eq: ambient connections SL dentro Mat} 
d_X Y|_A = D_X Y|_A + \langle{X,Y}\rangle\cdot A \in T_A\mathrm{Mat}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})~.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lem-18 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Decomposing  $d_X Y |_A \in T_A \mathrm{Mat}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ with respect to the direct sum decomposition $T_A \mathrm{Mat}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}) \cong T_A \operatorname{\mathrm{SL}}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}) \oplus \mathrm{Span}_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}(A)$, the component along $\mathrm{Span}_{\operatorname{\mathbb{C}}}(A)$ is characterized by the following identity:
$$
\langle{d_X Y|_A, A}\rangle = X(\langle{Y,\mathrm{Id}}\rangle)|_A - \langle{Y, d_X \mathrm{Id}}\rangle|_A = -\langle{Y, d_X\mathrm{Id}}\rangle|_A= -\langle{X,Y}\rangle .
$$
Moreover, the tangent component to $\operatorname{\mathrm{SL}}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ is equal to $D_X Y|_A$, where $D$ is the holomorphic Levi-Civita connection of $\mathrm{SL(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})}$.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
We locally lift $\sigma_t$ to $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)$, and we denote  by $\mathtt I_t$, $\mathtt {II}_t$, and $N_t$ the corresponding fundamental forms and normal vector fields. Recalling that
$$\dot\sigma=\left.\frac d {dt}\right|_{t=0}\sigma_t=fN~,$$
and observing that, as a consequence of Equation~\eqref{eq: ambient connections SL dentro Mat}, for every $X \in\Gamma(\operatorname{\mathbb{C}} T S)$,
                                                              
$$
d_X N:=d_{\mathrm{d}\sigma(X)} N= D_{\mathrm{d}\sigma(X)} N =-\mathrm{d}\sigma(B(X)) ,
$$
               
we compute:

\begin{align*}
    \dot \mathtt I(X,Y) &=\left.\frac d {dt}\right|_{t=0} \langle{d_X\sigma_t, d_Y\sigma_t}\rangle \\ &= \langle{d_X\dot \sigma, d_Y\sigma}\rangle+ \langle{d_X\sigma, d_Y\dot\sigma}\rangle \\
    &=\langle{\mathrm{d}f(X)N + fd_X N, d_Y\sigma}\rangle+ \langle{d_X\sigma, \mathrm{d}f(Y)N +fd_Y N}\rangle\\
    &=f\langle{d_X N, d_Y\sigma}\rangle+ f\langle{d_X\sigma,d_Y N}\rangle\\
    &=f\mathtt I(-B(X),Y)+f\mathtt I(X,-B(Y)) \\
    &=-2f \mathtt {II}(X,Y)~.
\end{align*}    

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
 

To compute the infinitesimal variation of $\mathtt {II}_t$, we first show the following formula for the infinitesimal variation of $N_t$: 
$$\dot N= f\sigma - \mathrm{grad}f~,$$
where $\mathrm{grad} f$ denotes the complex gradient vector field associated with the function $f$. 
To see this, we differentiate the identities $\langle N_t,N_t\rangle=1$, $\langle N_t,\sigma_t\rangle=0$ and $\langle N_t,\mathrm{d}\sigma_t(X)\rangle=0$, to obtain $\langle{\dot N, N}\rangle=0$, $\langle{\dot N, \sigma}\rangle=-\langle{N, \dot \sigma}\rangle= -f$ and 
$$\langle{\dot N, \mathrm{d}\sigma(X)}\rangle= -\langle{N, \mathrm{d}\dot \sigma (X)}\rangle= - \langle{N, \mathrm d f(X) N + f D_X N }\rangle= -\mathrm df(X)~.$$ 
This implies the formula.

Therefore, the infinitesimal variation of the second fundamental form is given by the following computation:
        \begin{align*}
        \dot{\mathtt {II}}(X,Y) & = - \left. \frac{d}{dt} \right|_{t=0} \langle{d_X\sigma_t, D_Y N_t}\rangle \\
        & = - \left. \frac{d}{dt} \right|_{t=0} \langle{d_X \sigma_t, d_Y N_t}\rangle \\
        & = - \langle{d_X \dot \sigma, d_Y N}\rangle - \langle{d_X \sigma, d_Y \dot N}\rangle \\
        &=- \langle{\mathrm{d}f(X) \cdot N + f d_X N, d_Y N}\rangle - \langle{d_X \sigma, -d_Y \mathrm{grad} f + \mathrm{d}f(Y) \cdot \sigma + f d_Y\sigma}\rangle \\
        &=- \langle{fd_X N, d_Y N}\rangle + \langle{d_X \sigma, \mathrm{d}\sigma(\nabla_Y^{\mathtt I} \mathrm{grad} f)}\rangle - \langle{d_X \sigma,f d_Y \sigma}\rangle \\
        &=-f \mathtt I(B(X), B(Y))+(\operatorname{\mathrm{Hess}}_{\mathtt I} f)(X,Y) - f \mathtt I(X,Y) ,
    \end{align*}
    where, in the second-to-last equality, we observed that $\langle N, d_Y N \rangle = Y(\langle N, N \rangle) = 0$. By taking the trace of the last expression with respect to the first fundamental form $\mathtt I$, we also obtain the identity:
    \[
    \mathrm{tr}_{\mathtt I}(\dot{\mathtt {II}}) = - f \mathrm{tr}(B^2) + \Delta_{\mathtt I} f - 2 f .
    \]
    
    To compute the infinitesimal variation of the mean curvature $\dot H_\sigma$, we observe that (formally, we treat $\mathtt I_t$ and $\mathtt {II}_t$ as matrices here, with respect to a local frame, since the result does not depend on the frame)

     \[
    \dot H_\sigma =\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|_{t=0} \mathrm{tr}_{\mathtt I_t}\mathtt {II}_t= \mathrm{tr}_{\mathtt I} \dot \mathtt {II} + \mathrm{tr}\left(\dot{(\mathtt I^{-1})}\mathtt {II}\right). 
    \]
    
                                                                                                                                                                            
       
                                                                                                                                             
       
  By the above computation, $\dot \mathtt I=-2f\mathtt {II}$, and since $\dot{(\mathtt I^{-1})}=-(\mathtt I^{-1})\dot\mathtt I (\mathtt I^{-1})$, we obtain
$$\mathrm{tr}\left(\dot{(\mathtt I^{-1})}\mathtt {II}\right)=2f\tr\left((\mathtt I^{-1}\mathtt {II})\right)=2f\tr(B^2)~.$$
   In conclusion, $ \dot H_\sigma= f \cdot \mathrm{tr}(B^2) -2f +\Delta_{\mathtt I} f$ as claimed.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- cor-7: body_md -->
Let $\Sigma$ be an oriented surface, let $\sigma:\Sigma\to \mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$ be a positive minimal immersion in $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$, such that the first fundamental form is of the form $\mathtt I:=\varrho h$ for $h$ a positive complex metric of constant curvature $-1$ and $\varrho\colon \Sigma\to \operatorname{\mathbb{C}}^*$ a smooth function, and the second fundamental form is of the form $\mathtt {II}=(q_1+\overline{q_2})/2$ for $q_1\in \operatorname{\mathrm{QD}}(\Sigma,J_1)$ and $\overline{q_2}\in \operatorname{\mathrm{QD}}(\Sigma,-J_2)$.
   
   Given $f\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\operatorname{\mathbb{C}})$, if we set $$\sigma_t(p):=\exp_{\sigma(p)}(tf(p)N(p))~.$$
    then the derivative of the mean curvature of $\sigma$ satisfies
  
    $$\left. \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \right|_{t=0} H_\sigma =\varrho^{-1}\Delta_{h}f +  \frac{2q_1\overline {q_2}}{\varrho^2h^2}f -2f $$
<!-- end cor-7 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
It suffices to apply Lemma~\ref{lemma: formula variation H}, taking into account that $\Delta_{\mathtt I}=\varrho^{-1}\Delta_h$ and, by the Cayley-Hamilton theorem $B^2=-\det(B)\mathrm{id}$ so that $\tr(B^2)=-2\det(B)=-2\det_{\mathtt I}\mathtt {II}=2(q_1\overline{q_2})/(\varrho^2 h^2)$, where the last identity has been verified in the proof of Corollary \ref{cor: GC semplificato}.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
